concepts.title: Values and types
concepts.summary: Programs manipulate values; types describe which values are allowed and which operations make sense on them.
objectives: Distinguish primitive values from structured values such as objects and arrays
Explain why static type annotations and assertions are erased at runtime, and contrast them with runtime checks
Predict the result of common type coercions, numeric edge cases (NaN, floating-point rounding), and nullability checks
misconceptions: Believing static type annotations still exist or are checked when the program runs
Treating null, undefined, empty string, and zero as interchangeable
Assuming a type assertion such as `as` converts a value rather than only silencing the type checker
Believing floating-point numbers represent decimal amounts such as 0.1 or currency exactly

intro.title: Why null, undefined, empty string, and 0 are four different answers
intro.focus: Builds the basic picture: a value is either a primitive (number, string, boolean, null, undefined) or a structured value (object, array), and each 'empty-looking' primitive means something different. This comes first because later lessons on checks and coercion depend on seeing these as separate values.
intro.check: Given `const a = 0; const b = ''; const c = null; const d = undefined; const e = { count: 0 };` which values are primitives and which is structured? For each one, predict what `typeof` returns and whether `x == null` is true.

applied.title: Why `as User` doesn't turn an API response into a User
applied.focus: Shows that type annotations and assertions are removed before the code runs. An assertion like `as` or `!` only quiets the checker and does not convert anything, while a check such as `typeof x === 'number'` actually runs. The learner applies this to data crossing into typed code. How to design validation for external input belongs to input validation, not this lesson.
applied.check: `const data = JSON.parse(body) as { age: number }; const next = data.age + 1;` The compiler accepts this, but body's age field is the string '42'. Predict the runtime value of `next`, then trace why the annotation did not stop it and which runtime check would have noticed.

advanced.title: How 0.1 + 0.2, NaN, and Number('') slip past a passing type check
advanced.focus: Covers edge cases that the type `number` allows: binary floating-point rounding, NaN (which is not equal to itself), and conversions like `Number('')` giving 0 or `parseInt('12px')` giving 12. The learner explains why code with correct types can still compute the wrong value.
advanced.check: `const total = [0.1, 0.2].reduce((s, x) => s + x, 0); if (total === 0.3) applyDiscount();` and `const qty = Number(input.trim());` with input '  '. Trace whether applyDiscount runs and what qty ends up as. Explain why both values are still typed `number`.

defense.title: Defend how `discount: number | null` behaves when the value is missing
defense.focus: This concept has no design or defend mode, so the learner explains out loud why a value's type matches what actually exists at runtime. They decide whether null and 0 should mean different things, weigh an assertion against a runtime check, and name the specific runtime value that breaks each option.
defense.check: This PR declares `discount: number | null` and computes `(row.discount as number) * price`. Explain whether null and 0 should mean different things here and what the multiplication produces at runtime when discount is null. Then argue for or against replacing the assertion with an explicit check, naming one tradeoff of your choice.

concepts.title: Control flow
concepts.summary: Conditionals, loops, and early returns decide which statements run and in what order.
objectives: Trace which branch of a conditional executes for given inputs
Explain how early returns and guard clauses change the reachable paths through a function
Identify off-by-one and non-terminating loop conditions
misconceptions: Assuming a JavaScript/C-style switch case without break stops at the end of that case
Believing a chain of conditionals covers every input when some inputs match no branch
Believing `if (value)` skips only null or undefined, when it also skips 0, empty string, and false

intro.title: Which branch runs? Reading an if/else-if chain for a specific input
intro.focus: Teaches reading a conditional chain top to bottom: the first matching branch runs and the rest are skipped. It also shows that some inputs can match no branch at all. This is the base skill for every later path-tracing lesson.
intro.check: `let grade; if (score > 90) grade = 'A'; else if (score > 80) grade = 'B'; else if (score >= 0) grade = 'C';` Predict `grade` for score = 90 and for score = -5.

applied.title: How an early `if (!qty) return` quietly skips a valid zero
applied.focus: Applies guard clauses and early returns to realistic functions: once a guard returns, the lines after it cannot run for those inputs. It shows that a truthiness guard also turns away 0, '' and false, not just null or undefined.
applied.check: `function setQuantity(item, qty) { if (!qty) return; item.qty = qty; save(item); }` An item has qty 3. Predict its qty after `setQuantity(item, 0)` and after `setQuantity(item, undefined)`, and trace which lines run in each call.

advanced.title: Tracing `<=` bounds, missing breaks, and loops that never exit
advanced.focus: Looks at how control flow fails in practice: off-by-one loop bounds, while loops whose exit condition never becomes true, and switch cases that fall through when `break` is missing. The learner traces these step by step and explains the result.
advanced.check: `for (let i = 0; i <= items.length; i++) sum += items[i].price;` with two items: trace `i` on each iteration and say what happens on the last one. Then, for `switch (status) { case 'paid': ship(); case 'refunded': refund(); }` with status 'paid', explain which functions run and why.

defense.title: Justify this function's branches: which inputs reach no branch at all?
defense.focus: This concept has no design or defend mode, so the learner explains out loud why a branching structure makes every input's path clear. That means finding inputs no branch handles and arguing for throwing, a default value, or an exhaustive switch, including what each one costs.
defense.check: This PR maps `plan` ('free' | 'pro' | 'team') to a limit using an if/else-if chain with no final else. Explain which inputs reach no branch (for example a new 'enterprise' plan or an empty string) and what the function returns for them. Then argue whether a guard clause that throws, a default value, or an exhaustive switch fits best here, and state one cost of your choice.

concepts.title: Functions and calls
concepts.summary: Functions package behavior behind parameters and return values; calling one creates a new frame of execution.
objectives: Trace arguments into parameters and return values back to the caller
Explain the call stack and what happens when a function calls another
Distinguish pure functions from functions with side effects
misconceptions: Believing a block-bodied function such as `function f() { x + 1 }` or `() => { x + 1 }` returns its last expression, as a concise arrow body would
Assuming a function with side effects returns the same result every time it is called with the same arguments

intro.title: Where arguments go and what comes back from one function call
intro.focus: Builds the model of a call: arguments are bound to parameters, the body runs, and only an explicit `return`, or a concise arrow body, sends a value back. A block body without `return` gives the caller undefined.
intro.check: `const addTax = (price) => { price * 1.2 };` Predict what `addTax(10)` returns, and pick which of two edits makes it return 12: removing the braces, or adding `return` inside them.

applied.title: What the call stack holds when `total` calls `shipping`
applied.focus: Applies the call stack to nested calls: each call gets its own frame, and the caller pauses until the callee returns. Tracing a path that returns nothing shows how an implicit undefined reaches the caller.
applied.check: `function total(items) { return subtotal(items) + shipping(items); }` `function shipping(items) { if (items.length > 3) return 0; }` subtotal returns 30. List the stack frames present while `shipping` runs, then predict what `total` returns for a two-item cart.

advanced.title: Why calling the same function twice can give two different answers
advanced.focus: Separates pure functions, whose result depends only on their arguments and which have no side effects, from functions that read or change outside state or do I/O. The learner sees why the second kind cannot safely be cached or reasoned about by argument alone.
advanced.check: `let calls = 0; function nextInvoiceNumber(prefix) { calls++; log(prefix); return prefix + calls; }` Trace two calls to `nextInvoiceNumber('INV-')` and give each return value. Explain which lines are side effects and why a caller cannot cache the result by argument.

defense.title: Defend where this function's side effects live
defense.focus: This concept has no design or defend mode, so the learner explains out loud a decision about function boundaries: whether to separate pure computation from side-effecting calls. They name what each choice costs callers and the failure it prevents or allows.
defense.check: This PR's `calculateRefund(order)` computes the amount, writes an audit log, and calls the payments API. Explain which parts are pure. Then argue whether to split the computation from the side effects, naming one cost of splitting and one failure mode of not splitting (for example, a caller that only wants a preview amount also triggers the payment call).

concepts.title: Scope and closures
concepts.summary: Scope determines which names are visible where; closures let functions keep access to variables from where they were created.
objectives: Predict which binding a name refers to in nested scopes
Explain how a closure captures variables rather than values
Recognize stale-closure and module-level shared-state bugs
misconceptions: Believing a closure snapshots a variable's value when created, rather than keeping a live reference to the variable
Believing a callback created in an earlier render or call sees later state, when it closed over a binding that was replaced rather than reassigned
Assuming module-level state is per request on a server
Confusing block scope with function scope (e.g. `var` in loops shared across iterations)

intro.title: Which `status` does this line see? Resolving names in nested scopes
intro.focus: Teaches how a name is looked up from the innermost scope outward. It shows why `let`/`const` are scoped to their block while `var` is scoped to the whole function, which changes which binding a name refers to.
intro.check: `let status = 'outer'; function run() { if (true) { let status = 'inner'; } return status; }` Predict what `run()` returns. Then predict the result if the inner `let` is changed to `var`.

applied.title: Why every timer in this loop logs the same index
applied.focus: Applies the key rule: a closure keeps a live reference to a variable, not a copy of its value. The learner traces a `var` loop that shares one binding across iterations against a `let` loop that creates a new binding on each iteration.
applied.check: `for (var i = 0; i < 3; i++) setTimeout(() => console.log(i), 0);` Predict the output. Predict it again with `let i`, and trace which binding each callback closed over in both versions.

advanced.title: Stale callbacks and module-level caches shared by every request
advanced.focus: Covers two failure modes. First, a callback created in an earlier render or call holds a binding that has since been replaced, so it sees old state. Second, module-level variables on a server are shared by every request the process handles, not kept per request.
advanced.check: `const cache = {}; export function handler(req) { cache.discount ??= req.user.discount; return price * (1 - cache.discount); }` User A (discount 0.2) and then user B (discount 0) hit the same server process. Trace the discount applied to B and explain why.

defense.title: Defend how this callback gets fresh state instead of a stale closure
defense.focus: The learner compares ways to give a long-lived callback current state and argues for one out loud, naming each alternative's failure mode. This shows they understand what was captured and when.
defense.check: This PR's `useEffect` runs `setInterval(() => setCount(count + 1), 1000)` with an empty dependency array. Explain what value of `count` the callback sees on every tick. Then compare three fixes (adding `count` to the dependencies, the updater form `setCount(c => c + 1)`, and reading from a ref), defend one, and name a failure mode or cost of each alternative.

concepts.title: Mutation and references
concepts.summary: Some values are shared by reference; changing them in one place changes them everywhere they are referenced.
objectives: Predict when two variables refer to the same underlying object
Explain the difference between shallow and deep copies
Evaluate when immutability prevents a class of bugs
misconceptions: Believing spread syntax performs a deep copy
Assuming const makes an object immutable
Believing sort or reverse return a new array and leave the original unchanged
Assuming passing an object or array to a function gives the function its own copy

intro.title: When two variables point at the same array
intro.focus: Builds the model that objects and arrays are passed and assigned by reference. A function that receives one can change the caller's data, because it gets no copy of its own.
intro.check: `function addDefault(tags) { tags.push('new'); return tags; } const original = ['a']; const result = addDefault(original);` Predict the contents of `original` after the call and whether `result === original`.

applied.title: Why `{ ...order }` still shares `order.items` with the original
applied.focus: Applies shallow and deep copying to realistic nested data: spread copies only the top level, so nested objects are still shared. It also shows that `const` stops reassignment of the variable but does not stop changes to the object.
applied.check: `const order = { id: 1, items: [{ sku: 'A', qty: 1 }] }; const copy = { ...order }; copy.id = 2; copy.items[0].qty = 5;` Trace `order.id` and `order.items[0].qty` afterward. Does declaring `order` with `const` change either answer?

advanced.title: How an in-place `sort()` reorders data other code still reads
advanced.focus: Looks at in-place methods (`sort`, `reverse`, `splice`) that change the array and return that same array. It shows how that leaks into data other code holds and into state stores that detect changes by comparing references, and the learner explains which bugs immutability rules out.
advanced.check: `const sorted = props.rows.sort((a, b) => a.date - b.date); setRows(sorted);` where `props.rows` is the same array already in state. Trace what happens to `props.rows`. Explain why a setter that compares with `Object.is(prev, next)` may skip the update.

defense.title: Defend copy, freeze, or build-new for this shared defaults object
defense.focus: The learner compares strategies for protecting shared data and defends one. They say what it costs and what it still does not protect against, for example that `Object.freeze` is shallow and, outside strict mode, silently ignores writes.
defense.check: This PR builds per-request settings with `const settings = { ...DEFAULTS }` and then sets `settings.limits.max = user.max`. Explain what this does to `DEFAULTS` for later requests. Then compare a deep copy (for example `structuredClone`), building a new nested object without mutation, and `Object.freeze(DEFAULTS)`, defend one, and name its cost and a case it does not cover.

concepts.title: Error handling
concepts.summary: Errors signal that an operation could not complete; handling them well means deciding where to recover, report, or propagate.
objectives: Trace how a thrown error propagates up the call stack
Distinguish expected failures from programming bugs
Evaluate whether a catch block recovers, translates, or silently hides a failure
misconceptions: Believing catching an error means the failure was handled
Believing that throwing a new error in place of the original loses nothing useful for debugging
Assuming finally only runs on success

intro.title: Where a thrown error goes when no one catches it right away
intro.focus: Builds the model of propagation: a throw leaves the current function right away, skips the rest of each frame, and is caught by the nearest enclosing catch up the stack. A finally block runs whether the try succeeds, throws, or returns.
intro.check: `function a() { b(); console.log('after b'); } function b() { throw new Error('boom'); } try { a(); console.log('after a'); } catch (e) { console.log('caught'); } finally { console.log('done'); }` Predict every printed line, in order.

applied.title: A missing user and a broken lookup are different kinds of failure
applied.focus: Applies the difference between expected failures, such as a missing record or invalid user input, and programming bugs. It shows how one broad catch that returns a default makes the two look identical to the caller.
applied.check: `function getEmail(id) { try { const user = users.get(id); return user.email.toLowerCase(); } catch { return null; } }` Predict what the caller receives when (a) no user has that id and (b) `users` is undefined because of a config bug. Explain which case is an expected outcome and which is a bug the catch is hiding.

advanced.title: Recover, translate, or hide: judging what a catch block really does
advanced.focus: Evaluates catch blocks by their effect: recovering, translating into a domain error while keeping the cause, or hiding the failure. The learner traces what debugging information survives each version.
advanced.check: Compare two catch blocks around `parseConfig(text)`: (1) `catch (e) { throw new Error('Invalid config'); }` and (2) `catch (e) { throw new ConfigError('Invalid config', { cause: e }); }`. Trace what a developer reading the logged error can learn about the original SyntaxError in each case.

defense.title: Defend where this failure is caught: here, the caller, or the top level
defense.focus: The learner defends where a catch belongs. They separate failures to handle locally from bugs that should propagate, and compare what the caller and an on-call engineer gain or lose under each placement.
defense.check: This PR catches every error from `chargeCard()` inside the service, logs it, and returns `{ ok: false }`. Defend whether that catch belongs here or higher up: which failures (a declined card vs. a bug such as an undefined variable) should be handled here, which should propagate, and what callers and on-call engineers lose or gain under your choice compared with the alternative.

concepts.title: Modules and boundaries
concepts.summary: Modules group related code behind an explicit interface so the rest of a program depends on what it exports, not how it works.
objectives: Explain what a module's public interface is and why it should be small
Predict module initialization order and side effects at import time
Evaluate whether a dependency direction between modules makes sense
misconceptions: Assuming importing a module has no side effects
Treating every exported symbol as a stable contract by accident
Believing circular imports are always harmless

intro.title: What this module promises: reading its exports as a contract
intro.focus: Introduces a module's public interface: anything it exports can become something other files depend on. A small, intentional interface lets the internals change without breaking callers.
intro.check: `pricing.ts` exports `calculateTotal`, `roundCents`, `TAX_TABLE`, and `_debugCache`. Which of these can other files now depend on, and which look internal? Explain what could break for callers if `TAX_TABLE`'s shape changes.

applied.title: Why importing `config.ts` runs code before your own file does
applied.focus: Applies module evaluation order: a module's top-level code runs once, the first time it is imported, before the importing module's own body runs. That makes importing a place where side effects like reading environment variables or opening connections can happen.
applied.check: `config.ts`: `console.log('config'); export const port = Number(process.env.PORT);` `server.ts`: `import { port } from './config'; console.log('server');` `index.ts`: `import './server'; console.log('index');` Predict the log order when running index.ts and when `process.env.PORT` is read. Explain what changes if `index.ts` also imports `./config` directly.

advanced.title: When a circular import hands you an uninitialized binding
advanced.focus: Covers circular imports: under native ES modules, reading an imported `const` before its module has finished running throws a ReferenceError, while deferring the read into a function can hide the cycle. The learner compares dependency directions that remove the cycle.
advanced.check: Native ES modules, entry `a.js`. `a.js`: `import { b, describe } from './b.js'; export const a = 'A' + b; console.log(describe());` `b.js`: `import { a } from './a.js'; export const b = 'B'; export function describe() { return a; }` Predict the output. Then predict what happens if `b.js` also runs `console.log(a)` at top level, and compare two ways to break the cycle.

defense.title: Defend this dependency direction and what the module exports
defense.focus: The learner defends a boundary decision. They weigh the interface each option makes someone keep stable, the direction of dependencies, and the import-time or cycle risk that remains.
defense.check: This PR makes `orders/` import a helper from `billing/internal/rates.ts`, while `billing/` already imports `orders/`. Argue for one fix: moving the helper to a shared module, exporting it from billing's entry point, or inverting the dependency by passing rates in. Explain what each option adds to a public interface someone must keep stable, and what cycle or import-time risk remains.

concepts.title: Synchronous vs. asynchronous work
concepts.summary: Asynchronous code starts work that finishes later, letting a program wait on I/O without stopping everything else.
objectives: Explain what it means for a program to wait on network or disk work
Predict execution order around await, promises, and callbacks
Identify an un-awaited promise and its consequences for errors and ordering
misconceptions: Believing await blocks the whole process
Believing a surrounding try/catch will catch the rejection of a promise that is never awaited
Believing `forEach` or similar callback APIs wait for async callbacks to finish before continuing

intro.title: What your server does while `await fetch()` is waiting
intro.focus: Builds the mental model of I/O waiting. `await` pauses only the current async function and hands control back to the event loop. The process keeps running timers and other callbacks until the result arrives.
intro.check: A handler runs `const res = await fetch(url)` and the network response takes 2 seconds. During those 2 seconds, can the same Node process run a pending timer callback? Explain what the awaiting function is doing meanwhile.

applied.title: Predicting log order around `await`, `.then`, and `setTimeout`
applied.focus: Applies execution-order rules: synchronous code finishes first, then promise continuations (microtasks) run, then timer callbacks. The code after an `await` always runs later, even when the awaited value is already available.
applied.check: `console.log(1); setTimeout(() => console.log(2), 0); Promise.resolve().then(() => console.log(3)); (async () => { console.log(4); await null; console.log(5); })(); console.log(6);` Predict the output order and trace why 6 logs before 5.

advanced.title: Why `forEach(async ...)` doesn't wait, and its errors escape try/catch
advanced.focus: Covers promises nobody waits on (floating promises): APIs like `forEach` ignore the promise a callback returns, so the code after them runs early. A try/catch around code that never awaits a promise cannot catch that promise's rejection, which becomes an unhandled rejection.
advanced.check: `async function saveAll(items) { try { items.forEach(async (item) => { await db.save(item); }); console.log('saved'); } catch (e) { console.log('failed'); } }` One `db.save` rejects. Trace when 'saved' logs relative to the saves, whether 'failed' ever logs, and what happens to the rejection.

defense.title: Defend awaiting, returning, or deliberately not awaiting this promise
defense.focus: The learner defends a choice about one promise: await it, return it, or fire and forget with an explicit rejection handler. They compare what each option means for ordering, error visibility, and what users and logs would see when the call fails.
defense.check: This PR calls `sendReceiptEmail(order)` without `await` after committing the order, so the response returns sooner. Defend whether to await it, return it, or keep it fire-and-forget with a `.catch` handler. Explain what happens to a rejection and to ordering in each option, and what the user and your logs would observe when the email service is down.

concepts.title: Dates, times, and time zones
concepts.summary: An instant in time, a calendar date, and a local wall-clock time are different things; confusing them causes off-by-hours and off-by-a-day bugs.
objectives: Distinguish an instant (UTC timestamp) from a calendar date and a local wall-clock time
Predict how a date is parsed, displayed, or compared across server and client time zones
Explain where time-zone conversion should happen when storing and displaying times
misconceptions: Believing a date-only string such as "2024-03-10" is parsed in local time by JavaScript's Date
Assuming every day has 24 hours in local time
Believing storing local time without a zone preserves the moment an event happened

intro.title: A timestamp, a birthday, and '9:00 AM' are different kinds of time
intro.focus: Builds the vocabulary: an instant is a single moment, usually a UTC timestamp; a calendar date has no time or zone; a local wall-clock time only means a moment once a zone is known. A local time stored without its zone does not pin down when something happened.
intro.check: Classify each field as an instant, a calendar date, or a local wall-clock time: `createdAt: 1710057600000`, `birthDate: '1990-04-12'`, `storeOpensAt: '09:00'`, `meetingStart: '2024-03-10 14:00'` (no zone). Explain which ones cannot become a single moment without more information.

applied.title: Why `new Date('2024-03-10')` shows March 9 for users in New York
applied.focus: Applies parsing rules in JavaScript: a date-only ISO string is parsed as UTC midnight, while a date-time string with no offset is parsed as local time. The learner predicts what users in different time zones see.
applied.check: On a machine set to America/New_York, predict `new Date('2024-03-10').getDate()` and `new Date('2024-03-10T00:00').getDate()`. Trace which string is parsed as UTC and which as local time.

advanced.title: Adding 24 hours isn't 'tomorrow' on a daylight-saving change day
advanced.focus: Covers date arithmetic around daylight-saving changes: local days can be 23 or 25 hours long, so adding milliseconds (moving the instant) and adding a calendar day (moving the local date) give different results. This matters for expiry and start-of-day logic.
advanced.check: In America/New_York: `const start = new Date(2024, 2, 9, 12, 0); const next = new Date(start.getTime() + 24 * 60 * 60 * 1000);` Trace `next`'s local date and hour. Explain why `start.setDate(start.getDate() + 1)` gives a different local hour.

defense.title: Defend where this app converts time zones: storage, API, or display
defense.focus: The learner defends a storage-and-conversion design. They compare a UTC instant with a local wall-clock time plus an IANA zone ID, match the choice to what the data means (a past event vs. a recurring local appointment), and name the failure mode of the rejected option.
defense.check: This PR stores `appointment_at` in a `timestamp` (without time zone) column filled from the server's local time, and the client formats it with `toLocaleString()`. Explain what moment is actually recorded when servers run in different zones. Compare storing a UTC instant (`timestamptz`) with storing a local wall-clock time plus an IANA zone ID, defend which fits a recurring 9:00 AM appointment, and name the failure mode of the option you reject.

concepts.title: Arrays and lists
concepts.summary: Ordered collections that support indexed access and iteration; the default structure for sequences of data.
objectives: Trace common array transformations such as map, filter, and reduce
Explain the cost of inserting or removing at the front versus the end
Identify when a linear scan over a list becomes a performance concern
misconceptions: Assuming includes, find, or indexOf are constant-time lookups
Treating indexOf's -1 not-found result as falsy, or a found index of 0 as not found
Believing reduce without an initial value is safe on an empty array
Believing slice and splice both leave the original array unchanged

intro.title: What slice, splice, map, and filter do to the array you passed in
intro.focus: Builds the mental model of which array operations return a new array and which change the original in place, using map, filter, slice, and splice on tiny inputs. At this depth the goal is reliably predicting the before-and-after values of short snippets.
intro.check: Given `const a = [1, 2, 3, 4]; const b = a.slice(1, 3); const c = a.splice(1, 2);`, predict the values of a, b, and c after the second line and again after the third line.

applied.title: Why `if (list.indexOf(id))` skips item 0 and empty reduce throws
applied.focus: Applies transformation tracing to realistic pipelines and to their edge values: an indexOf result of 0 or -1, and reduce over an array that filter may have emptied. The learner traces chained map/filter/reduce and predicts the not-found and empty cases, not only the happy path.
applied.check: `const total = carts.filter(c => c.active).map(c => c.price).reduce((sum, p) => sum + p);` Trace what happens when no cart is active. Then predict whether the body of `if ([7, 8].indexOf(7)) { ... }` runs.

advanced.title: Why unshift, front splice, and includes slow down as arrays grow
advanced.focus: Examines the hidden per-call cost of array operations: inserting or removing at the front or middle shifts every later element, and includes/find/indexOf scan element by element instead of looking anything up directly. The learner explains why an operation that is fine on a 10-item fixture behaves differently on a 100,000-item array.
advanced.check: A PR builds a newest-first feed with `for (const msg of incoming) feed.unshift(msg);` and skips duplicates with `if (!feed.includes(msg)) ...`. For 50,000 messages, explain roughly how many element moves and comparisons happen per call as the feed grows, and why appending with push and reversing once behaves differently.

defense.title: Defend this linear scan, or name the list size where you'd stop
defense.focus: The learner justifies out loud whether a linear scan over a list is acceptable in their context, weighing list size, how often it runs, and where it sits (request path vs. startup), and states what evidence would change their answer. The lesson has no design mode, so the work is a spoken tradeoff argument, not a rewrite.
defense.check: A request handler calls `users.find(u => u.id === id)` on an in-memory list loaded at startup. Explain whether this scan is acceptable today, what list size or call frequency would make it a concern, what you would measure before changing it, and why 'find is a built-in, so it's fast' isn't a sufficient argument.

concepts.title: Maps and sets
concepts.summary: Key-based structures, usually hash tables, that answer 'have I seen this key?' and 'what value belongs to this key?' in expected constant time; sorted tree-based maps trade that for ordered keys and logarithmic lookup.
objectives: Choose between an array, a set, and a map for a lookup-heavy task
Explain how key equality works for objects versus strings
Refactor a nested-loop lookup into a map-based lookup
misconceptions: Expecting object or array keys in a Map or Set to be matched by their contents rather than by reference
Assuming every map or dictionary iterates in insertion order (true for JavaScript Map and Python dict, false for Go maps, Java HashMap, Postgres jsonb keys, and integer-like keys on plain JS objects)
Believing a plain JavaScript object is a safe dictionary for arbitrary user-supplied keys such as __proto__ or constructor

intro.title: Why `new Set([{ id: 1 }, { id: 1 }])` has size 2
intro.focus: Builds the mental model that a Set answers 'have I seen this key?' and a Map answers 'what value goes with this key?', and that keys are compared by value for primitives but by reference for objects. At intro depth the learner recognizes which structure fits a lookup and predicts membership results.
intro.check: `const seen = new Set(); seen.add('42'); seen.add(42); seen.add({ id: 1 }); seen.add({ id: 1 });` Predict `seen.size`, `seen.has(42)`, and `seen.has({ id: 1 })`.

applied.title: Replacing a find() inside map() with a lookup Map built once
applied.focus: Applies maps to a realistic join: turning a nested find-per-item lookup into a Map built once by ID, then tracing the misses that come from key mismatches such as string vs. number IDs or array-valued composite keys. Goes beyond intro by making the learner own the refactor and its not-found behaviour.
applied.check: `orders.map(o => ({ ...o, user: users.find(u => u.id === o.userId) }))` Rewrite this to build a Map from users once, trace the result for an order whose userId has no matching user, and explain what the lookup returns if user IDs are numbers but order.userId values are strings like '7'.

advanced.title: When a plain object keyed by user input is not a safe dictionary
advanced.focus: Covers failure modes of choosing the wrong key-value structure: plain objects treat keys like '__proto__' and 'constructor' specially and put integer-like keys first when enumerating, while Date or object keys in a Map match only the same instance. The learner compares a plain object, Object.create(null), and Map for untrusted keys.
advanced.check: A PR stores preferences with `const prefs = {}; prefs[req.body.key] = req.body.value;` and later lists them with `Object.keys(prefs)`. Compare this with `Object.create(null)` and `new Map()`: explain what each does for the keys '__proto__', '10', and '2', and which choice avoids each problem.

defense.title: Defend your lookup structure, including what it promises about order
defense.focus: The learner justifies choosing an array, Set, hash Map, or sorted tree-based map for a real task, weighing lookup cost, ordered output, and whether code downstream depends on iteration order that another language or storage layer does not guarantee. With no design/defend mode available, the defense is a compare-and-explain argument out loud.
defense.check: Your PR keeps about 50 feature flags in a JavaScript Map keyed by name, and an admin page lists them in the Map's iteration order, expecting creation order. Defend your choice among an array, a Map, and a sorted (tree-based) map. Cover lookup cost, how you would produce reliably ordered output, and what breaks if the same data is later read from a Go map or a Postgres jsonb column.

concepts.title: Stacks and queues
concepts.summary: Structures that define processing order: last-in-first-out for stacks, first-in-first-out for queues.
objectives: Distinguish LIFO and FIFO processing and predict output order
Trace an iterative traversal that uses an explicit stack, and predict how the visit order changes when the stack is swapped for a queue
Explain why dequeuing from the front of a plain array slows down as the queue grows, and name a structure that avoids it
misconceptions: Confusing stack order with queue order, e.g. expecting push/pop to process items in arrival order
Believing an array-backed queue that dequeues with shift stays cheap as the queue grows
Believing that replacing recursion with an explicit stack removes the memory cost of deeply nested input, rather than moving it from the call stack to the heap

intro.title: push/pop hands back the newest item; push/shift the oldest
intro.focus: Builds the core LIFO vs. FIFO mental model with a single array used two ways, so the learner can predict output order before reading any traversal code. Intro depth: recognize which discipline a snippet uses and predict what comes out first.
intro.check: `const s = []; s.push('a'); s.push('b'); s.push('c');` Predict what `console.log(s.pop(), s.pop())` prints, and what `console.log(s.shift(), s.shift())` would print instead if run on a fresh copy of the same array.

applied.title: How swapping pop() for shift() changes a work list's visit order
applied.focus: Applies LIFO/FIFO to an iterative traversal that uses an explicit work list. The learner traces visit order step by step with a stack, then again with a queue, and explains why the stack version visits siblings in reverse push order.
applied.check: Menu: root has children [A, B]; A has child A1; B has none. Loop: `const work = [root]; while (work.length) { const n = work.pop(); visit(n.name); work.push(...(n.children ?? [])); }` Trace the visit order, then trace it again with `work.shift()` in place of `work.pop()`.

advanced.title: Why a shift()-drained queue slows down as the backlog grows
advanced.focus: Examines the cost of dequeuing from the front of a plain array or Python list: each removal can move every remaining element, so draining a large backlog does far more work than the item count suggests. The learner compares a head-index pointer, a ring buffer, and a deque as replacements.
advanced.check: An in-process queue can hold 200,000 pending items and is drained with `while (queue.length) handle(queue.shift());` (or `items.pop(0)` in Python). Explain why each dequeue can cost time proportional to the remaining length, and compare a head-index pointer, a ring buffer, and `collections.deque` as fixes, including what each costs in memory or complexity.

defense.title: Does an explicit stack really make deep input safe? Defend your claim
defense.focus: The learner evaluates a decision to replace recursion with an explicit stack. They explain that this moves per-level state from the call stack to the heap without removing it, name the failure mode that remains, and defend what extra guard, if any, the code needs. Justification is done with the highest available modes (explain/compare).
defense.check: A PR replaces a recursive walker over uploaded JSON with an explicit stack, and the description says 'deeply nested input can no longer crash the service'. Evaluate that claim: explain where the memory for a document nested 1,000,000 levels deep now lives, what can still fail, and compare adding a depth or size limit against leaving the code as is.

concepts.title: Recursion
concepts.summary: A function that solves a problem by calling itself on smaller instances until it reaches a base case.
objectives: Identify the base case and the progress toward it
Trace a recursive call on a small input
Explain the risk of stack overflow on deep or untrusted inputs
misconceptions: Believing Node.js (V8) or Python optimizes tail calls, so a tail-recursive function cannot overflow the stack
Assuming every input eventually reaches the base case, overlooking cyclic references or values that move away from it
Assuming recursion depth is safe because typical inputs are shallow, when nesting depth is controlled by users

intro.title: Find the base case, then check every input actually moves toward it
intro.focus: Builds the mental model of recursion as 'solve a smaller version, stop at a base case' and teaches the learner to find the base case and the step that makes progress. Includes inputs that step past or away from the base case, so termination is checked rather than assumed.
intro.check: `function countdown(n) { if (n === 0) return; countdown(n - 1); }` Identify the base case and the progress step, then predict what happens for `countdown(3)`, `countdown(-1)`, and `countdown(2.5)`.

applied.title: Tracing a recursive tree-depth call, and what one cycle does to it
applied.focus: Applies recursion to realistic nested data. The learner traces calls and return values frame by frame on a small input, then predicts what happens when the data contains a reference cycle and no call ever reaches the base case.
applied.check: `function depth(node) { return 1 + Math.max(0, ...node.children.map(depth)); }` Trace depth(root) where root.children = [A, B], A.children = [C], and B and C have `children: []`. Then predict what happens if C.children is set to [root].

advanced.title: Why a tail-recursive walker still overflows in Node.js and Python
advanced.focus: Covers the stack-depth failure mode. Every call uses a stack frame, V8 (Node.js) and CPython do not perform tail-call elimination, and passing tests on small fixtures say nothing about how deep real input can go. The learner explains when and how the code fails (RangeError in Node.js, RecursionError in Python).
advanced.check: `function last(node) { return node.next ? last(node.next) : node; }` runs on a linked list built from a user-uploaded file with 200,000 nodes. Explain whether this can throw in Node.js, why having the call in tail position does not help, and why a passing test suite built on 50-node fixtures does not show it is safe.

defense.title: Who controls the nesting depth? Defend recursion or a depth cap here
defense.focus: The learner justifies aloud whether recursion is acceptable for a specific input source. They state what guarantees termination, who controls the depth, what happens at the limit, and which guard they would choose and why. No defend/design mode exists, so the defense is a structured explanation of the tradeoff.
defense.check: Your PR recursively evaluates a user-submitted search filter made of nested AND/OR groups. Explain whether recursion is an acceptable choice: what guarantees each call reaches a base case, what nesting depth a hostile client could send, what the service does when the stack limit is hit, and which guard you'd choose (a depth limit during validation, a request size limit, or an iterative rewrite) and why.

concepts.title: Time and space complexity
concepts.summary: Big-O describes how work and memory grow with input size, which predicts where code will fall over at scale.
objectives: Estimate the time complexity of nested loops and chained collection operations
Explain why an O(n²) algorithm can be fine for small n and catastrophic for large n
Identify hidden linear work inside a loop, such as includes or spread-copying an accumulator
misconceptions: Treating Big-O as a measure of actual runtime
Ignoring memory growth when counting only time
Assuming library calls are constant time

intro.title: Counting how often the inner line runs when loops are nested
intro.focus: Builds the mental model that Big-O describes how the amount of work grows with input size, not how many milliseconds it takes. The learner counts operations in nested loops and predicts how the count changes when inputs double.
intro.check: `for (const o of orders) for (const r of refunds) if (o.id === r.orderId) count++;` With 1,000 orders and 500 refunds, predict how many comparisons run, and by what factor that number changes if both lists double in size.

applied.title: Why includes() inside filter() is a nested loop in disguise
applied.focus: Applies loop counting to realistic chained collection code, where the inner loop is hidden inside a library call. The learner traces the real amount of work and explains why chaining map, filter, and map is still linear, while a scan inside a callback is not.
applied.check: `const fresh = incoming.filter(x => !existingIds.includes(x.id)).map(toRow);` Trace roughly how many comparisons happen in the worst case with 10,000 incoming items and 10,000 existing IDs, and explain which call hides the inner loop and why the trailing `.map` does not change the growth rate.

advanced.title: When spreading the reduce accumulator makes time and memory quadratic
advanced.focus: Covers growth that code review misses: copying an accumulator on every iteration costs quadratic time and creates a lot of short-lived memory, and O(n²) code passes review on small fixtures but breaks at production sizes. The learner compares time and space costs of alternatives instead of looking at running time alone.
advanced.check: `const byId = rows.reduce((acc, r) => ({ ...acc, [r.id]: r }), {});` Explain why total work grows roughly with n², describe the memory churn it causes, and compare it with mutating a single accumulator. Then explain why it looked fine on a 20-row fixture but not with 50,000 rows.

defense.title: Keep the O(n²) or pay for O(n)? Design for the sizes you'll really see
defense.focus: The learner designs a change for a workload with a known range of sizes and defends it. They weigh time against memory, argue when a quadratic algorithm is acceptable, and state the measurement that would confirm the choice, without treating Big-O as a runtime prediction.
defense.check: A PR loads an entire export into an array (usually 300 rows, but some customers have 2M) and removes duplicates with a nested loop. Propose a design that limits both time and memory, compare it with keeping the current code, and defend your choice. Say what you would measure before shipping and why Big-O alone cannot tell you the runtime.

concepts.title: Trees
concepts.summary: Hierarchical structures such as file systems, DOMs, ASTs, and B-tree indexes, traversed depth-first or breadth-first.
objectives: Trace depth-first and breadth-first traversals on a small tree
Explain how tree height affects lookup cost
Recognize tree structures hiding in nested data such as comments or categories
misconceptions: Assuming nested data such as comments or categories is always shallow
Assuming parent/child data loaded from a database or user input is guaranteed acyclic, so traversal needs no visited set or depth limit
Believing every tree gives logarithmic lookup regardless of balance

intro.title: Spotting the tree hiding in a parent_id column
intro.focus: Builds the mental model of a tree (root, parent, children, leaf, depth) and teaches the learner to recognize trees in everyday data such as self-referencing foreign keys and nested JSON. Also shows that the data, not the developer's expectation, decides how deep a tree goes.
intro.check: A categories table has rows (1, Root, null), (2, Books, 1), (3, Fiction, 2), (4, Sci-Fi, 3), (5, Music, 1), (6, Jazz, 5) as (id, name, parent_id). Identify the root and the leaves, and predict how many levels deep Sci-Fi is if Root counts as level 1.

applied.title: Why deleting a folder tree must visit children before their parent
applied.focus: Applies traversal to a realistic task. The learner traces preorder, postorder, and breadth-first visit order on a small tree and picks the order an operation needs, such as postorder for deleting children before their parent.
applied.check: Tree: Root has children [Docs, Img]; Docs has children [a.txt, b.txt]; Img has child [c.png]. Trace the visit order for preorder DFS, postorder DFS, and BFS. Then say which order a `deleteNode` call needs if it fails on non-empty folders.

advanced.title: Guarding a tree walk against a cycle someone saved to the database
advanced.focus: Covers failure modes when tree-shaped data isn't a valid tree: a bad parent_id edit creates a cycle, or user-made nesting grows far deeper than expected. The learner traces what a naive walk does and compares a visited set, a depth limit, and a cycle check at write time.
advanced.check: A breadcrumb builder follows parent_id upward until it reaches null. An admin sets category 4's parent to 7, and 7 is already a descendant of 4. Trace what the walker does, then compare a visited set, a maximum depth, and a cycle check at save time: what each catches, and what each costs.

defense.title: Defend the 'O(log n) lookups' claim for a tree built from sorted IDs
defense.focus: The learner judges a claim about lookup cost by reasoning about tree height. They explain why an unbalanced tree built from sorted keys degrades toward a linked list, compare it with a balanced tree or a high-fanout B-tree index, and defend what the code should use. Done with the highest available modes (compare/explain).
defense.check: A PR adds a hand-written binary search tree, fills it with 100,000 IDs that arrive already sorted, and says lookups are O(log n). Compare the resulting height and worst-case lookup cost with a balanced tree and with a B-tree index. Then defend whether the PR should keep its tree and what you would use instead.

concepts.title: Searching and sorting
concepts.summary: Ordering data and finding items in it efficiently, including binary search and stable comparison-based sorting.
objectives: Explain why binary search requires sorted input
Predict the outcome of a custom comparator, including stability
Choose between sorting in the database and sorting in application code
misconceptions: Believing default JavaScript sort compares numbers numerically
Believing a comparator may return a boolean instead of a negative, zero, or positive number
Assuming a query without ORDER BY returns rows in insertion or primary-key order
Believing binary search over unsorted or differently sorted data will fail loudly rather than silently return a wrong result

intro.title: Why `[10, 9, 1, 100].sort()` returns [1, 10, 100, 9]
intro.focus: Builds the mental model that sorting depends entirely on the comparison it uses. JavaScript's default sort compares values as strings, and a numeric comparator changes the result. The learner predicts sort output before learning comparator contracts in detail.
intro.check: Predict the result of `[10, 9, 1, 100].sort()` and of `[10, 9, 1, 100].sort((a, b) => a - b)`, and explain in one sentence why they differ.

applied.title: Comparators return a number, not a boolean, and ties keep their order
applied.focus: Applies the comparator contract (negative, zero, or positive) to realistic sort keys. The learner predicts why a boolean comparator gives unreliable order, and uses stable sort (guaranteed for Array.prototype.sort since ES2019) to predict where tied items end up.
applied.check: Tasks `[{id: 'a', p: 2}, {id: 'b', p: 1}, {id: 'c', p: 2}]` are sorted with `(x, y) => x.p > y.p`. Predict whether the result is guaranteed to be ordered by p. Then trace `(x, y) => x.p - y.p` and state whether 'a' or 'c' comes first.

advanced.title: Binary search on differently sorted data quietly returns wrong answers
advanced.focus: Covers why binary search needs input sorted by the same ordering it compares with. The learner traces the probes on data that is sorted differently (for example, case-insensitively) and explains why the search returns a plausible wrong result instead of raising an error.
advanced.check: Python's `bisect_left(names, 'bob')` runs on `['Alice', 'bob', 'Carol', 'dave']`. The list was sorted case-insensitively, but bisect uses default string ordering, where uppercase letters sort before lowercase. Trace each midpoint probe, state the index it returns, and explain why a membership check built on it misses 'bob' without raising an error.

defense.title: Sort in SQL or in the app? Defend where ordering and top-N belong
defense.focus: The learner defends where ordering and limiting should happen. They weigh row volume, pagination stability when sort keys tie, collation differences between the database and application code, and the fact that a query without ORDER BY guarantees no order. Done with the highest available modes (compare/explain).
defense.check: A PR runs `SELECT * FROM invoices WHERE customer_id = $1` (no ORDER BY), sorts the rows in JavaScript by created_at, and returns the first 20 as page one. Defend whether ordering and the limit should move into the query. Cover how many rows get fetched, what happens to pagination when created_at values tie, differences between SQL collation and localeCompare, and what order the current query actually guarantees.

concepts.title: HTTP request lifecycle
concepts.summary: A request message (method, URL, headers, body) passes through server routing and middleware to handler code, and a response (status, headers, body, possibly streamed) travels back, with failure or client disconnection possible at every hop.
objectives: Trace a request from a client call through middleware to a handler and back
Explain where headers, body, and status are set and read
Identify where latency and failures can occur along the path
misconceptions: Believing a request either fully succeeds or fully fails
Assuming middleware runs for every route regardless of registration order or matcher configuration
Believing server-side work automatically stops when the client disconnects

intro.title: Following one request from fetch() through middleware to a handler
intro.focus: Builds the mental model of a request as a message that passes through ordered middleware to a handler, and a response built from status, headers, and body. Introduces the idea that registration order and matchers decide which middleware a route actually passes through.
intro.check: An Express app registers app.use(logger), then app.get('/health', (req, res) => res.send('ok')), then app.use(requireAuth). A client sends GET /health. Predict which of logger, the /health handler, and requireAuth run, and in what order.

applied.title: Why a stream that fails halfway still arrives with a 200 status
applied.focus: Applies the lifecycle to realistic handler code: where status and headers are committed, why they cannot change once the body starts streaming, and how a request can end in a partial result rather than clean success or failure.
applied.check: A handler calls res.writeHead(200, {'Content-Type': 'text/csv'}), streams 3 of 10 rows from a database cursor, then the cursor throws. Trace what status code the client receives, what the body contains, and how the client could tell the export is incomplete.

advanced.title: Why the server keeps working after the user closes the tab
advanced.focus: Examines failure and latency at each hop, focusing on client disconnection: by default handler work continues unless code observes an abort signal and passes it to downstream calls that support cancellation.
advanced.check: A handler awaits a 20-second report query, writes the result to a cache, then sends the response. The client aborts after 2 seconds. Trace which steps still run, then explain what changes if the handler checks request.signal and passes it to a query client that supports cancellation, and what still runs if the driver does not.

defense.title: Buffer or stream through a proxy: explaining where each one fails
defense.focus: The learner explains out loud how the choice of buffering versus streaming at a proxy hop changes latency, memory, and which partial failures the client can observe. They also justify what a client may safely conclude from each outcome.
defense.check: Your service proxies file uploads to a storage service. Compare buffering the whole body before forwarding with streaming it through as it arrives. For each, explain where latency accumulates, what the client sees if the upstream fails after receiving half the bytes or if the client disconnects mid-upload, and what a 502 does and does not tell the client about upstream state.

concepts.title: HTTP methods and status codes
concepts.summary: Methods declare intended semantics (safe, idempotent, or neither) that servers must actually honor; status codes tell clients and intermediaries what happened and whether retrying or caching makes sense.
objectives: Distinguish safe, idempotent, and non-idempotent methods
Choose appropriate status codes for validation, auth, conflict, and server errors
Explain how status codes drive client retry and caching behavior
misconceptions: Believing a failure reported only in a 200 response body will be treated as a failure by clients, caches, retries, and monitoring
Believing 403 is the right response when credentials are missing or invalid, or 401 when an authenticated user lacks permission
Assuming fetch rejects on 4xx and 5xx responses
Believing a GET handler that changes state is harmless because only your own UI calls it

intro.title: Safe, idempotent, or neither: what GET, PUT, DELETE, and POST promise
intro.focus: Introduces method semantics as promises the server must honor: safe methods should not change state, idempotent methods have the same effect when repeated. It shows why a state-changing GET breaks those promises for crawlers, link prefetchers, and caches.
intro.check: Classify each handler as safe, idempotent but not safe, or neither: GET /orders, PUT /users/42/email, DELETE /carts/7, POST /orders, and GET /unsubscribe?id=9, which sets subscribed = false on a row.

applied.title: Why fetch resolves on a 500 and your catch block never runs
applied.focus: Applies status codes to real client code: fetch rejects only on network-level failures, so the client has to check response.ok or response.status. Also shows how retry and caching logic branch on that status.
applied.check: Client code: try { const r = await fetch('/api/save', { method: 'POST' }); showToast('Saved'); } catch { showToast('Failed'); }. The server responds 500. Predict which toast appears and explain what change makes the client treat the response as a failure.

advanced.title: 401, 403, 404, 409, or 422: status codes that tell clients the truth
advanced.focus: Covers the edge cases in choosing codes for auth, permission, conflict, and validation outcomes, including the tradeoff of returning 404 instead of 403 so a resource's existence isn't revealed.
advanced.check: For PATCH /projects/9, choose a status for each case and explain what the client should do next: no session cookie; valid session but the user is not a project member; project 9 does not exist; the request carries a stale version number; the name field is empty. Where two codes are defensible, compare them.

defense.title: Defending real status codes against 'always return 200 with ok:false'
defense.focus: The learner argues out loud, with tradeoffs, how the status-code contract affects intermediaries and tooling that never read the body, including caches, retry layers, load balancers, and error-rate monitoring.
defense.check: A teammate proposes returning 200 with { ok: false, error } for every failure so the frontend has one code path. Compare this with meaningful status codes: explain how each choice affects a CDN caching GET responses, a client retry policy that retries on 5xx, and an alert on 5xx error rate. Then state which you would ship and what it costs.

concepts.title: Serialization and JSON
concepts.summary: Turning in-memory values into bytes for transport or storage and back again, and what gets lost along the way.
objectives: Predict how dates, big integers, undefined, NaN, and Maps survive a JSON round-trip
Identify precision loss when 64-bit IDs or decimal amounts pass through JSON or floating-point numbers
Identify accidental over-exposure of fields in serialized responses and compare explicit response mapping with returning database objects directly
misconceptions: Assuming large integer IDs or decimal money values survive JSON and floating-point numbers without precision loss
Believing Dates round-trip through JSON as Date objects
Believing fields the UI does not display are not exposed to users

intro.title: What JSON.stringify quietly drops: undefined, NaN, Maps, and Dates
intro.focus: Builds the mental model that JSON has only strings, numbers, booleans, null, arrays, and objects, so richer in-memory values are converted or dropped on the way out. None of them come back as their original type.
intro.check: Predict the result of JSON.parse(JSON.stringify({ at: new Date(0), note: undefined, score: NaN, tags: new Map([['a', 1]]) })), including the type of each surviving property.

applied.title: Why order 9007199254740993 comes back as 9007199254740992
applied.focus: Applies round-trip reasoning to IDs and money: a JSON number parsed into an IEEE-754 double loses integer precision above 2^53 and cannot represent most decimal fractions exactly. The lesson traces where the corruption happens.
applied.check: A Java service serializes a 64-bit order ID 9007199254740993 as a JSON number, and a JavaScript client parses it with JSON.parse and then requests GET /orders/{id}. Trace the value at each step and predict which ID the follow-up request uses. Then predict what 0.1 + 0.2 displays for a price total computed in the client.

advanced.title: Returning the ORM row: how passwordHash ends up in the API response
advanced.focus: Examines over-exposure: everything in the serialized payload reaches the client regardless of what the UI renders. Returning whole database objects also means future schema changes silently change the response.
advanced.check: A handler does res.json(await db.user.findUnique({ where: { id } })) and the profile page shows only name and avatar. Trace which fields reach the browser's network tab, and explain what happens to this response when a teammate later adds a resetToken column to the users table.

defense.title: Response mappers vs. serialized models: defending your wire format
defense.focus: The learner weighs an explicit mapping layer against serializing models directly, covering field exposure, ID and decimal encoding, date representation, and maintenance cost. They justify a choice and name what it still leaves unprotected.
defense.check: Compare a hand-written toPublicOrder() mapper that emits id as a string, amount as integer minor units, and createdAt as an ISO-8601 string with returning the ORM model plus a global toJSON override. Explain which you would choose for a public API, what each costs to maintain, and one failure each approach still permits.

concepts.title: REST resource design
concepts.summary: Modeling an API as resources with consistent URLs, methods, and representations so clients can reason about it.
objectives: Evaluate whether routes model resources or leak implementation actions
Compare REST resources with RPC-style endpoints or framework RPC mechanisms (e.g. server actions, tRPC) for a given use case
Design error and versioning conventions an API can keep
misconceptions: Believing a response field can be renamed or removed safely because the frontend was updated in the same deploy
Believing resource URLs should name actions (e.g. POST /deleteUser) rather than resources acted on by HTTP methods
Assuming each endpoint can use its own ad-hoc error shape without cost to clients

intro.title: From POST /deleteUser to DELETE /users/{id}: naming resources
intro.focus: Introduces the idea of modeling URLs as nouns acted on by HTTP methods instead of verbs baked into paths. It explains what clients and tooling can infer from a consistent resource structure.
intro.check: An API exposes POST /createOrder, GET /getOrders, and POST /cancelOrder?id=5. Explain how these would look if they modeled an orders resource, and what a client can infer from the resource version that it cannot from the action names.

applied.title: Why renaming a response field breaks clients you already shipped
applied.focus: Applies API evolution to a realistic change: deploying frontend and backend together does not update clients already in the field, so a representation is a contract. It compares additive changes with versioning.
applied.check: A PR renames user_name to displayName in the GET /users/{id} response and updates the web app in the same deploy. Explain which consumers can still break (for example, open browser tabs running the old bundle, installed mobile apps, partner integrations), and compare shipping it as an additive field with deprecation against introducing a new API version.

advanced.title: One error envelope or many: designing errors clients can handle
advanced.focus: Covers the hidden cost of per-endpoint error shapes and how to design one error convention, such as RFC 9457 problem details, that validation, conflict, and not-found cases can all share and keep using.
advanced.check: Three endpoints return errors as { error: 'msg' }, { errors: [{ field, msg }] }, and a plain-text body. Design a single error envelope that covers field-level validation, a conflict, and a missing resource, including a stable machine-readable code. Compare its cost to leaving the shapes ad hoc for a client that calls all three.

defense.title: REST resource or server action? Defending the endpoint style you chose
defense.focus: The learner defends a choice between a REST resource and an RPC-style mechanism (server action, tRPC procedure, or action endpoint) for a specific use case, weighing consumers, caching, versioning, and discoverability.
defense.check: Your PR adds a server action archiveProject(id) called only from your Next.js app. Defend this choice against PATCH /projects/{id} with a status field and POST /projects/{id}/archive. Say who the consumers are today, how each option handles versioning and caching, and what future requirement would make you switch.

concepts.title: Authentication vs. authorization
concepts.summary: Authentication establishes who is making a request; authorization decides whether that identity may perform this action on this resource.
objectives: Distinguish identity verification from permission checks in a handler
Identify endpoints that authenticate but never check ownership or role
Explain where authorization must be enforced server-side and why client checks are insufficient
misconceptions: Believing a logged-in user may access any resource whose ID they know
Believing hiding a button or page in the UI prevents the underlying endpoint from being called
Believing an authentication check in middleware also enforces per-resource permissions in every handler

intro.title: Who are you vs. may you do this: spotting the two checks in a handler
intro.focus: Builds the distinction between authentication (establishing identity) and authorization (deciding whether that identity may act on this resource), and shows that a handler can do the first without the second.
intro.check: A handler runs const user = await requireSession(req); then const doc = await db.document.findUnique({ where: { id: req.params.id } }); then returns doc. Label which line authenticates, and predict whether any line decides if this user may read this document.

applied.title: Why knowing an invoice ID shouldn't be enough to read it
applied.focus: Applies the distinction to a realistic endpoint that authenticates but loads by ID alone, letting any logged-in user read other users' records. It shows how scoping the lookup by owner or tenant changes the outcome.
applied.check: User A is logged in and requests GET /invoices/1043, which belongs to user B. The handler verifies the session, then runs findUnique({ where: { id: 1043 } }). Predict the response, then explain how filtering by ownerId or tenantId changes it and which status the handler should return instead.

advanced.title: Hidden buttons, open endpoints: where authorization has to live
advanced.focus: Examines failure modes where authorization exists only in the UI or only as a coarse middleware session check. It covers why the server must enforce permissions per action and per resource.
advanced.check: An admin-only Delete workspace button renders only when user.role === 'admin', and middleware only verifies that a session exists. Explain what a non-admin member can do with curl against DELETE /workspaces/:id. Compare enforcing the role in middleware by path, in the handler, or in a shared policy function called from the handler.

defense.title: Defending an authorization design that new endpoints can't forget
defense.focus: The learner designs and defends how per-resource permission checks are enforced across many handlers, weighing inline checks, a central policy layer, and tenant-scoped data access. They anticipate how each design can still be bypassed.
defense.check: A multi-tenant API has 40 handlers and is adding more. Design how authorization is enforced, and defend your choice against inline checks in every handler, a central policy function, and tenant-scoped query helpers or database row-level security. Describe one concrete way a newly added endpoint could still skip the check under your design.

concepts.title: Pagination
concepts.summary: Returning large collections in bounded pages, using offsets or cursors, so responses stay fast and consistent.
objectives: Compare offset and cursor pagination under concurrent inserts
Explain why unbounded list endpoints become availability risks
Design a stable sort order for cursor pagination
misconceptions: Assuming offset pagination never skips or duplicates rows
Believing a timestamp or other non-unique column alone gives a stable cursor order
Assuming a single call to a paginated API returns the complete result set
Letting clients request arbitrarily large page sizes

intro.title: Why page 2 can repeat an item you already saw
intro.focus: Builds the mental model of offset pagination as 'skip N rows of the current result', so inserts or deletes between page requests shift which rows land on each page. Cursors are introduced as the contrast.
intro.check: A feed sorted newest-first uses LIMIT 10 OFFSET 10. After the client loads page 1 (posts 1-10), three new posts are inserted at the top. Predict which posts page 2 returns, then predict what happens if instead two posts from page 1 are deleted.

applied.title: The sync job that only imported the first 100 customers
applied.focus: Applies pagination to realistic code on both sides of a call: a consumer must follow next-page tokens until done, and a provider must cap page size so no single request can load the whole table.
applied.check: A nightly job calls a third-party GET /customers?limit=100 once and upserts the results. The response includes has_more: true and next_cursor. There are 2,350 customers. Predict how many are imported. Then explain what your own GET /customers endpoint should do when a client sends ?limit=1000000.

advanced.title: created_at alone isn't a cursor: ties, skipped rows, and tiebreakers
advanced.focus: Examines why a cursor needs a total order: with a non-unique sort column, rows sharing the boundary value get skipped or repeated. Covers adding a unique tiebreaker and how that compares with offset under concurrent writes.
advanced.check: Rows are paged with WHERE created_at < :last_created_at ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20, and five rows share the timestamp at the page boundary. Explain which rows are skipped. Compare a composite cursor (created_at, id) backed by an index on those columns with switching back to offset pagination while new rows keep arriving.

defense.title: Designing a list endpoint that stays fast as the table keeps growing
defense.focus: The learner designs and justifies a complete list contract (limits, sort order, cursor format, what is given up) and explains the tradeoffs out loud. Pagination has no defend mode, so the justification happens through design and comparison.
defense.check: Design the contract for GET /events on a table growing by 1M rows per day: default and maximum page size, sort order and tiebreaker, cursor encoding, and behavior for an invalid cursor. Justify each choice and compare what you give up (jump-to-page, exact total counts) against offset pagination.

concepts.title: Retry strategies
concepts.summary: Re-attempting failed calls can mask transient faults, but only with limits, backoff, jitter, and awareness of what is safe to repeat.
objectives: Decide which failures are worth retrying and which are not
Explain exponential backoff and why jitter prevents synchronized retry storms
Identify retries that can duplicate side effects
misconceptions: Believing immediate, repeated retries help a struggling dependency recover
Treating every error as retryable, including 400 or 422 validation failures
Ignoring 429 responses and Retry-After hints when scheduling the next attempt
Assuming retries configured at several layers (client, SDK, server, queue) add up rather than multiply

intro.title: Why retrying a 422 will fail the same way every time
intro.focus: Builds the mental model that retries only help transient failures. A deterministic rejection such as a validation error will return the same answer on every attempt, while some network errors and 5xx responses may succeed later.
intro.check: A client retries any non-2xx response up to 3 attempts. Predict what each retry yields for (a) a 422 because email is missing, (b) a 503 during a rolling deploy, and (c) a 404 for a deleted record. State which retries could plausibly succeed.

applied.title: Why retrying a timed-out POST can charge the card twice
applied.focus: Applies retry reasoning to side effects. A timeout means the client doesn't know the outcome, not that the operation failed, so retrying a non-idempotent call can repeat work the server already committed.
applied.check: A client sends POST /payments with a 2-second timeout. The server commits the charge at 2.4s and would respond at 2.5s, but the client gives up at 2.0s and retries once, and the retry succeeds. Trace both attempts on a timeline and state how many charges exist.

advanced.title: Backoff, jitter, and Retry-After: spacing retries so services recover
advanced.focus: Examines retry timing as a load problem: immediate or synchronized retries amplify an outage. Exponential backoff with jitter spreads attempts out, and a 429 with Retry-After tells the client exactly when to try again.
advanced.check: 1,000 clients receive a 503 at the same instant and all retry with fixed exponential backoff (1s, 2s, 4s). Explain the request pattern the dependency sees. Compare it with full-jitter backoff, and with a client that receives 429 plus Retry-After: 30 but retries after 1s anyway.

defense.title: Retries at three layers: designing a budget that doesn't multiply
defense.focus: The learner designs a retry policy across stacked layers and justifies it. Attempts multiply across layers, so they decide where retries live, which errors each layer retries, and how backoff and caps bound worst-case load. Retries has no defend mode, so justification happens through design and comparison.
defense.check: A browser makes up to 3 attempts, the API gateway makes up to 3 attempts per incoming request, and the server's SDK makes up to 3 attempts against the database. Compute the worst-case database attempts for one user click. Then design where retries should live, which failures each layer retries, and the caps and backoff you would set. Compare your design with retrying only at the outermost layer.

concepts.title: Idempotency
concepts.summary: An idempotent operation has the same effect whether it runs once or many times, which is what makes retries safe.
objectives: Predict the outcome when two requests with the same idempotency key arrive concurrently or after a crash mid-processing
Design an idempotency-key scheme with an atomic uniqueness guard and a stored result for replays
Evaluate which operations in a workflow are naturally idempotent and which need protection
misconceptions: Believing POST requests cannot be made idempotent
Believing it is safe to record an idempotency key only after the side effect succeeds
Believing a handler whose state update is idempotent (e.g. set status = 'paid') is safe to repeat even though it also triggers emails, charges, or other side effects

intro.title: Same effect once or ten times: which operations are safe to repeat
intro.focus: Builds the definition of idempotency as the effect of repeated execution, not identical responses, and shows how to judge whether an operation is naturally idempotent. POST is not inherently non-idempotent; it just isn't idempotent by default.
intro.check: Each request is delivered twice. Predict the final state for PUT /users/7/email { email: 'a@x.com' }, DELETE /carts/3 (the second call returns 404), POST /counters/9/increment, and POST /orders, and mark which operations had the same effect as a single delivery.

applied.title: Status is 'paid' twice, but the customer got two receipts
applied.focus: Applies idempotency to a whole handler: an idempotent state update doesn't make the handler idempotent when it also sends emails, charges cards, or enqueues jobs on every run.
applied.check: A webhook handler runs UPDATE orders SET status = 'paid' WHERE id = $1, then calls sendReceiptEmail(order) and enqueues a fulfillment job. The provider delivers the same event twice. Predict the order's status, the number of emails, and the number of fulfillment jobs, and explain which steps need protection.

advanced.title: Two requests, one key: races and crashes in idempotency checks
advanced.focus: Examines the failure modes of naive key handling: check-then-act races when duplicates arrive concurrently, and keys recorded after the side effect, so a crash leaves no record that the work happened.
advanced.check: Handler: if (!(await keys.exists(k))) { const r = await charge(); await keys.insert(k, r); }. Predict the number of charges when (a) two requests with the same key arrive 5ms apart, and (b) the process crashes after charge() returns but before keys.insert. Compare with first inserting the key as 'in_progress' under a unique constraint.

defense.title: Defending an idempotency-key design against crashes and replays
defense.focus: The learner designs a complete idempotency-key scheme and defends it. It needs an atomic uniqueness guard, a stored result for replays, mismatch detection, and recovery for keys stuck mid-processing. The learner also admits what a local database cannot make atomic with an external side effect.
defense.check: Design an Idempotency-Key scheme for POST /payments: the uniqueness guard, what is stored and returned on replay, how you handle the same key with a different request body, and what happens to a key left 'in_progress' after a crash. Defend it against a Redis SET NX lock with a TTL, and say whether you would forward the key to the payment provider.

concepts.title: Same-origin policy and CORS
concepts.summary: Browsers stop scripts on one origin from reading responses from another unless the server opts in with CORS headers; CORS controls what browsers may read, not who can call the server.
objectives: Predict whether a cross-origin browser request is sent directly, preflighted, or sent but blocked from being read
Explain why CORS does not stop non-browser clients or protect an endpoint from being called
Identify unsafe CORS configurations such as reflecting any Origin while allowing credentials
misconceptions: Believing CORS is a server-side access control that blocks unauthorized callers
Believing reflecting the request Origin with credentials allowed is a safe fix for a CORS error
Assuming a request whose response was blocked by CORS never reached or changed anything on the server

intro.title: What CORS blocks: reading the response, not sending the request
