Assuming a hand-written mock's responses still match the real dependency after that dependency changes
Believing a test still exercises real logic after the code under test has itself been mocked or stubbed

intro.title: Stubs, spies, fakes, mocks: what each lets a test control
intro.focus: Introduces the kinds of test doubles by what they give the test: canned answers, recorded calls, or a working substitute. Also shows the trap of replacing the very code the test is meant to check.
intro.check: Test A replaces the email client with an object that records every `send()` call. Test B replaces the pricing client with one that always returns `{ price: 100 }`. Test C calls `vi.mock('./calculateDiscount')` and then asserts the discount from `calculateDiscount`. Name the kind of double in A and B, say what each lets the test control or check, and explain what real logic Test C no longer runs.

applied.title: When 'the mock was called once' is not proof the feature works
applied.focus: Applies doubles to realistic service code where call-count assertions stand in for outcome checks. Learners explain what an interaction assertion checks, what it misses, and when the result can be checked directly.
applied.check: A test for `createOrder(cart)` mocks the repository and asserts only `expect(repo.save).toHaveBeenCalledTimes(1)`. `createOrder` has a bug that computes the total without tax. Explain why the test still passes, and rewrite the assertion so it checks the outcome (the saved order's total) instead of just the call.

advanced.title: How a hand-written mock drifts from the real API and hides a break
advanced.focus: Examines the failure mode where a mock encodes an old assumption about a dependency, so the tests keep passing after the real dependency changes. Learners compare doubles by how likely they are to catch that drift.
advanced.check: Your payment client mock returns `{ status: 'ok' }`. After an SDK upgrade, the real client returns `{ state: 'succeeded' }`, and the code checking `status === 'ok'` now treats every payment as failed. All tests pass. Compare three options: the hand-written mock, a shared fake that is also run against the provider's sandbox, and an integration test against the sandbox. For each, which would catch the drift, and what would it cost?

defense.title: Mock, in-memory fake, or real database for this repository layer?
defense.focus: The learner chooses a double strategy for a data-access layer and defends it, naming real-database behavior each option cannot show and saying where the choice would stop being right.
defense.check: A signup service depends on a SQL repository that relies on a unique constraint on email. Design the tests for the service, choosing among a mocked repository, an in-memory fake, and a real database in a container. Defend your choice, explain whether a duplicate-email signup would be caught by each option, and describe when you would change your mind.

concepts.title: Logs, metrics, and traces
concepts.summary: Structured logs, metrics, and traces let you understand what production is doing without attaching a debugger.
objectives: Explain what a structured log line should contain to be useful in an incident
Distinguish when to use a log, a metric, or a trace
Identify logging that leaks sensitive data or is too noisy to use
misconceptions: Believing logs are internal, so it is safe to log tokens, passwords, or full request bodies
Believing more log lines always improve debuggability
Believing counting or rate questions are best answered by searching logs rather than recording a metric
Assuming unbounded values such as user IDs or raw URLs are fine as metric labels

intro.title: What a log line needs so you can use it during an incident
intro.focus: Builds the idea that a useful log is a structured event with context fields (request ID, entity IDs, error code), so it can be filtered and linked to other events, and that a few good events beat many vague lines.
intro.check: Compare `console.log('payment failed')` printed at five places in a handler with one `logger.error({ requestId, orderId, provider, errorCode }, 'payment failed')`. Which one lets you find every event for a single failing checkout, and which fields make that possible?

applied.title: How logging the full request body leaks passwords into your logs
applied.focus: Applies logging judgment to realistic middleware: finding secrets and personal data that end up in log storage, and logging so noisy it hides the signal. Learners explain the exposure and what to log instead.
applied.check: Middleware runs `logger.info({ headers: req.headers, body: req.body })` on every request, including POST /login, and a batch loop logs one info line per processed row (about 2M rows a night). Explain what sensitive data now sits in log storage and who can read it, why the loop logging makes incidents harder to debug, and what you would log instead.

advanced.title: Logs, metrics, or traces for 'how often' and 'where is it slow'
advanced.focus: Compares the three signals by the question each one answers well, including the cost trap of using high-cardinality metric labels. Suited to learners who can already write good logs.
advanced.check: The team wants (a) error rate per endpoint over the last week and (b) which downstream call makes checkout slow at p99. One proposal is to search logs for both. Another adds a counter labeled `{ endpoint, user_id }`. Compare log search, a counter or histogram, and a distributed trace for each question, and explain what a `user_id` label does to the metrics backend.

defense.title: Designing telemetry for a new endpoint without PII or label blowups
defense.focus: The learner designs logs, metrics, and spans for a real change and defends each choice: what to leave out, which label values stay bounded, and how the plan could still fail during an incident.
defense.check: A PR adds POST /exports, which queues a job that calls a storage service. Design its telemetry: log events with fields and levels, what you redact, metric names with labels whose values stay bounded, and trace spans. Justify one thing you chose not to record, and describe an incident question your design still could not answer.

concepts.title: Timeouts
concepts.summary: A timeout bounds how long code waits on something that may never answer, turning a hang into a handleable failure.
objectives: Identify outbound calls with no timeout
Explain how a slow dependency without timeouts can exhaust a service
Design timeout budgets across nested calls
misconceptions: Believing HTTP clients have sensible default timeouts
Believing Promise.race against a timer cancels the slower operation, when it keeps running and holding resources
Assuming aborting a request on the client stops work already running on the server or in the database
Believing an inner call's timeout can safely exceed the outer request's deadline because the caller will keep waiting

intro.title: Why an outbound call with no timeout can wait forever
intro.focus: Builds the mental model that a wait on the network has no built-in end, and that many clients default to no timeout or a very long one. Learners predict what an unbounded wait does to a single request.
intro.check: A server handler calls `await axios.get(inventoryUrl)` using axios defaults (timeout 0, meaning no timeout). The inventory service accepts the TCP connection but never sends a response. Predict what the caller's request is doing after 30 seconds and after 10 minutes, and what (if anything) will eventually end the wait.

applied.title: How one slow dependency ties up every worker in your service
applied.focus: Applies the idea at service level: calls that never time out hold pooled resources, so a slow dependency spreads into endpoints that never call it. Learners trace resource use over time.
applied.check: A service has a DB connection pool of 10. Each /quote request takes a connection, then calls a pricing API with no timeout before releasing it. The pricing API starts taking 60 seconds per call, and /quote gets 5 requests per second. Trace the pool's state at t=1s, 2s, and 3s, and explain what happens to /health and /orders, which only need a DB connection.

advanced.title: Promise.race timed out, but the slow query is still running
advanced.focus: Covers the gap between giving up on a wait and actually stopping the work. A race only rejects the caller's promise, an abort signal cancels the client-side request, and only a server-enforced limit stops the server's work.
advanced.check: `await Promise.race([db.query(reportSql), sleep(2000).then(() => { throw new Error('timeout') })])` runs a query that takes 30 seconds. Trace what the caller sees at 2s and what the query and its pooled connection are doing from 2s to 30s. Then compare that with passing `AbortSignal.timeout(2000)` to an HTTP call to a slow service, and with setting a database `statement_timeout`. Which one stops work on the server?

defense.title: Budgeting timeouts across nested calls under a 3-second deadline
defense.focus: The learner designs timeout budgets for a chain of calls and defends each value. The core rule is that no inner wait should outlast the deadline of the request it serves, so the design must pass the remaining time down the chain.
defense.check: A gateway gives up on requests after 3s. The handler calls auth (p99 80ms), then pricing, and pricing calls a tax service. Proposed timeouts are auth 1s, pricing 5s, tax 4s. Explain what happens when tax takes 3.5s, then design a budget and a way to pass the remaining deadline down the chain. Justify your numbers against the latency data, and name one failure mode your design still has.

concepts.title: Failure recovery
concepts.summary: When multi-step or background work fails partway, making the resulting state visible and recoverable: explicit failed states, bounded retries that end in a dead-letter or manual path, safe resumption, and honestly degraded responses.
objectives: Trace what state a workflow is left in when it fails at each step
Compare retrying, dead-lettering, and failing fast for a given failure
Design a recovery path for work that fails permanently
misconceptions: Assuming a failed job leaves no partial state
Believing enough retries will eventually succeed, so permanent failures never need a separate path
Believing silent fallbacks are safer than making degraded behavior visible to users and operators

intro.title: What a half-finished job leaves behind when step three throws
intro.focus: Builds the mental model that multi-step work fails in the middle and leaves partial state behind. Learners trace the state after each step to see what users and operators can actually observe.
intro.check: A checkout job (1) inserts an order with status 'pending', (2) charges the card through a payment API, (3) updates status to 'paid', and (4) sends a receipt email. Step 3 throws after step 2 succeeds. Trace the order row, the customer's card, and what the customer and an operator can each see. Then explain why 'the job failed, so nothing happened' is wrong.

applied.title: Retry, dead-letter, or fail fast: matching the response to the failure
applied.focus: Applies recovery choices to a realistic queue consumer. Temporary and permanent failures need different paths, and unlimited retries turn a permanent failure into an endless loop that hides it.
applied.check: A queue consumer retries without limit. It hits three failures: the provider returns 503, the message is missing a required field, and the card is declined. Trace what unlimited retries do to the malformed message over an hour. Then compare, for each failure, whether a bounded retry, a dead-letter queue, or failing fast with a recorded failed status is the right response.

advanced.title: Why a silent fallback can do more harm than an honest error
advanced.focus: Examines degraded responses: when fallbacks help, when stale or default data quietly misleads users, and how to keep a degraded mode visible to users and operators.
advanced.check: A product endpoint catches pricing-service errors and returns prices cached six hours ago with HTTP 200 and no indication. Compare three responses: the silent fallback, a fallback that marks the response as stale and increments a degraded-mode counter, and failing fast with 503. For each, explain what a customer placing an order and an on-call engineer would experience while pricing is down.

defense.title: Defending a recovery path for jobs that will never succeed
defense.focus: The learner designs a recovery path for permanent failures (explicit failed state, bounded attempts, dead-letter storage, safe replay) and defends it against simpler alternatives, including how the design itself could fail.
defense.check: A nightly job exports 50,000 invoices to an accounting API, and some invoices fail every night because their customer was deleted. Design how failed invoices are recorded, how attempts are capped, and how an operator replays them without re-exporting invoices that already succeeded. Defend your design against 'retry until it works' and 'skip it and write a log line', and name one way your design could still fail quietly.

concepts.title: Tests that can fail
concepts.summary: A test is evidence only if it would fail when the behavior breaks and gives the same result on every run; weak assertions and nondeterminism turn tests into noise.
objectives: Predict whether a test would fail if the behavior it describes were broken
Identify sources of nondeterminism in a test: wall-clock time, randomness, execution order, shared state, and un-awaited async work
Explain why a regression test should be seen failing before the fix is applied
misconceptions: Believing high code coverage means the important behavior is tested
Believing a passing test is evidence of correctness even though it has never been seen to fail
Treating a flaky test as noise to retry or skip rather than a sign of a race or hidden dependency
Assuming tests run in a fixed order with isolated state

intro.title: A test that passes no matter what the code does
intro.focus: Builds the core idea that a test is evidence only if it would fail when the behavior breaks. Learners spot weak assertions and predict whether a deliberately broken implementation would still pass.
intro.check: `it('applies SAVE10', async () => { const total = await applyDiscount(cart, 'SAVE10'); expect(total).toBeTruthy(); })` with a cart totaling 50. Predict: if `applyDiscount` ignored the code and returned 50, would this test fail? What assertion would make it fail?

applied.title: Coverage ran the line, but did any assertion notice the bug?
applied.focus: Applies the idea to realistic tests. Coverage records which lines ran, not what was checked, and an un-awaited assertion can finish after the test does. Learners also see why a regression test should be run against the unfixed code first.
applied.check: You fix an off-by-one in `paginate()` and add `it('pages', () => { expect(paginate(items, 2)).resolves.toHaveLength(10) })` without `await` or `return`. Coverage for `paginate` is 100%. Predict whether this test fails if you revert the fix, and explain what reverting the fix and running the test first would have shown you.

advanced.title: Flaky tests are pointing at a race or hidden shared state
advanced.focus: Examines where nondeterminism comes from: wall-clock time, randomness, run order, shared state, and un-awaited async work. Treats flakiness as a clue to a hidden dependency, not as noise.
advanced.check: Two test files import a module-level `users` array. File A pushes a user, and File B asserts `users.length === 0` at the start. A third test creates a token that expires at `new Date()` plus 24 hours and asserts it is 'valid tomorrow' using the calendar date. Predict the run orders and times of day when each test fails, and explain the hidden dependency behind each failure.

defense.title: Fix the flaky test or add CI retries? Making the call out loud
defense.focus: The concept has no design or defend mode, so the learner compares ways to handle a flaky test and explains their reasoning out loud, including how to confirm the stabilized test can still fail.
defense.check: A test that waits on a background job fails about one run in 20. One teammate proposes `retries: 3` in CI, another suggests raising the timeout to 10s, and a third wants to await the job's completion signal or use fake timers. Compare the three options: what each hides or reveals about the underlying race, which you would choose and why, and how you would check that the stabilized test still fails when the job's behavior is broken.

concepts.title: Networking basics
concepts.summary: DNS, TCP connections, TLS, and latency — the substrate every remote call depends on.
objectives: Trace what happens between resolving a hostname and receiving the first response byte
Explain why network calls are slower and less reliable than function calls
Identify connection reuse and pooling in client code
misconceptions: Treating a remote call like a local function call
Assuming the network is reliable and latency is zero
Disabling certificate verification to fix a TLS error

intro.title: Why calling an API is not like calling a local function
intro.focus: Builds the mental model that a remote call crosses a network. The network adds latency, can fail even when your code is right, and can hang. At this depth the learner only needs to spot which lines in their code leave the process.
intro.check: Which of these lines can take hundreds of milliseconds or fail even when the code is correct: `const total = add(a, b)`, `const user = await fetch('https://api.example.com/users/42')`, `const data = JSON.parse(text)`? Pick one and say why.

applied.title: Tracing a request from hostname lookup to first response byte
applied.focus: Walks through DNS resolution, the TCP handshake, the TLS handshake, sending the request and server processing. The learner can then tie latency and errors in their own outbound calls to a specific step.
applied.check: A freshly started process runs `await fetch('https://payments.internal/health')`. Trace, in order, what happens before the first response byte arrives, and name the step where each of these errors would occur: ENOTFOUND, ECONNREFUSED, and a certificate verification error.

advanced.title: Why opening a fresh connection per request costs latency and sockets
advanced.focus: Examines connection reuse with keep-alive agents and pools: which handshakes a reused connection skips and what happens under load without reuse. It also covers edge cases, such as a server closing an idle kept-alive connection or requests queuing when the pool is full.
advanced.check: Compare a client that creates a new HTTPS agent inside every request handler with one that reuses a single module-level agent with keepAlive enabled. At 200 requests/second to the same host, which one repeats the TCP and TLS handshakes per request, and what resource can the first one exhaust?

defense.title: Justifying a real fix when a TLS certificate error blocks a call
defense.focus: The learner explains out loud what certificate verification protects against. They weigh turning it off against fixing the real cause, and predict what breaks if a workaround reaches production.
defense.check: Staging calls fail with 'unable to verify the first certificate'. A teammate proposes `rejectUnauthorized: false`. Explain what that removes, compare it with supplying the internal CA bundle or fixing the server's incomplete certificate chain, and say what failure you would expect if the workaround shipped to production.

concepts.title: Configuration
concepts.summary: Separating environment-specific settings from code, and validating them before the application relies on them.
objectives: Explain why configuration should differ by environment while code stays the same
Identify configuration read lazily in a way that fails late in production
Design fail-fast validation for required settings
misconceptions: Silently defaulting a required production setting
Assuming build-time and runtime environment variables behave the same
Scattering environment reads throughout the codebase

intro.title: Why staging and production run the same code with different settings
intro.focus: Introduces configuration: values that change by environment (URLs, credentials, log levels) live outside the code and are read in one place. Rules that belong in code stay in code. The learner only needs to tell the two apart.
intro.check: Which of these should come from configuration rather than being written in code: the database hostname, a payment provider secret key, the maximum allowed username length, the log level? Explain your choice for one of them.

applied.title: How a missing environment variable can pass deploy and fail at checkout
applied.focus: Uses realistic code where a setting is read lazily inside a rarely used function and quietly given a default. The misconfiguration only shows up when a real user reaches that path.
applied.check: `function charge(order) { const key = process.env.PAYMENT_KEY ?? ''; return client(key).charge(order); }` is only called at checkout. If PAYMENT_KEY is unset in production, explain when the problem first surfaces, who notices, and what error they see.

advanced.title: Why editing a deploy-time variable doesn't change your built frontend
advanced.focus: Explores the case where a bundler inlines some variables at build time while others are read at runtime. This creates a tradeoff when you build one artifact and promote it across environments.
advanced.check: Client code reads `process.env.PUBLIC_API_URL`, which the bundler inlines at build time; a server route reads `process.env.API_URL` at runtime. One artifact is built, then both variables are changed at deploy time. Compare which value each code path uses and explain why.

defense.title: Designing a config module that refuses to start with bad settings
defense.focus: The learner designs central config loading that fails fast. They justify which settings may have defaults and which must stop the service at startup, and when a default really is the right call.
defense.check: Design startup config loading for a service needing DATABASE_URL, PORT, and PAYMENT_KEY: which get defaults, which stop the process at boot, how values are type-checked, and where the rest of the code reads them. Defend failing at startup over failing on first use, and give one setting where a default is appropriate.

concepts.title: Concurrency
concepts.summary: Making progress on several tasks over overlapping time periods, and the ordering and shared-state hazards that creates.
objectives: Explain how Promise.all changes execution, latency, and error behavior compared to sequential awaits
Identify race conditions in interleaved async operations
Distinguish concurrency from parallelism
misconceptions: Believing Promise.all cancels remaining work when one promise rejects
Assuming single-threaded runtimes have no race conditions across awaits
Believing a promise's work starts only when it is awaited, so creating several promises before awaiting them runs them one at a time

intro.title: Why back-to-back awaits take longer than starting both requests first
intro.focus: Builds the model that a promise's work starts when the async function is called, not when it is awaited. Starting two requests before awaiting either lets them overlap, even though JavaScript runs one callback at a time. That is concurrency without parallelism.
intro.check: `getUser()` and `getOrders()` each take about 100ms. Version A: `const u = await getUser(); const o = await getOrders();`. Version B: `const pu = getUser(); const po = getOrders(); const [u, o] = await Promise.all([pu, po]);`. Predict the approximate total time of each and when each request starts.

applied.title: What Promise.all does when one call fails and the others keep running
applied.focus: Applies Promise.all to realistic fan-out code. It rejects as soon as any input rejects, but the other operations are not cancelled: they run to completion and their results are thrown away. Contrasts this with allSettled.
applied.check: `await Promise.all([sendEmail(), chargeCard(), writeAudit()])`: chargeCard rejects at 50ms, writeAudit resolves at 120ms, sendEmail resolves at 200ms. Predict when the await throws and whether the email is still sent and the audit row still written.

advanced.title: How two async handlers can both pass a check before either updates
advanced.focus: Examines check-then-act races on in-memory state across an await. A single thread stops code from running at the same instant, but not from interleaving, so a shared variable can be read before another handler updates it.
advanced.check: Module-level `let seats = 1`. Handler: `if (seats > 0) { await reserveWithProvider(); seats--; }`. Two requests arrive at the same moment on one process. Trace the interleaving, then state how many reservations are made and the final value of seats.

defense.title: Defending sequential awaits, Promise.all, or allSettled for this handler
defense.focus: The learner chooses how to run several async operations and justifies it, weighing latency, error behavior and ordering dependencies. They also name the race or partial-completion hazard the design must still handle.
defense.check: An order handler charges a card, reserves inventory, and sends a receipt. Choose sequential awaits, Promise.all, or Promise.allSettled (or a mix), justify it on latency and error behavior, explain what keeps running if one call rejects, and describe how you avoid sending a receipt for a failed charge.

concepts.title: Processes and threads
concepts.summary: Operating-system units of execution: isolated processes, shared-memory threads, and how runtimes like Node map work onto them.
objectives: Explain how the event loop, worker threads, and separate processes differ
Predict what blocks the event loop and its effect on all requests
Choose between threads, processes, and separate services for CPU-heavy work
misconceptions: Believing async makes CPU-bound work non-blocking
Believing worker threads or subprocesses share ordinary in-memory variables with the main thread
Believing one slow synchronous request only delays itself, rather than every request on that instance

intro.title: Why one slow synchronous request stalls every other request
intro.focus: Builds the model that a Node process runs JavaScript on one event-loop thread. Synchronous work in one handler delays every request on that instance, not just its own.
intro.check: A Node server has `/hash`, which runs a synchronous loop taking 2 seconds, and `/health`, which returns immediately. A request hits /hash, and 100ms later another client calls /health. Predict roughly when /health responds.

applied.title: Why marking CPU-heavy work async doesn't stop it blocking
applied.focus: Separates waiting on I/O, which gives the event loop back (sometimes via the runtime's thread pool), from CPU work, which blocks whether or not it sits inside an async function. Applies this to parsing, hashing, and sync file or crypto calls in handlers.
applied.check: `async function parseReport(buf) { return JSON.parse(buf.toString()); }` is awaited in a handler with a 200MB upload. Predict whether other requests are served while it parses, and explain why the async keyword doesn't change that, whereas switching `pbkdf2Sync` to the callback `pbkdf2` does.

advanced.title: What a worker thread can and cannot see of your main thread's memory
advanced.focus: Compares the event loop, worker threads and child processes by how they handle memory. Each worker gets its own copy of every module and exchanges copied messages. SharedArrayBuffer is the exception, and passing large data has a copy cost.
advanced.check: The main thread imports `cache.js`, which exports `new Map()`, and starts a Worker whose script imports the same module and calls `cache.set('x', 1)`. After the worker finishes, predict what `cache.get('x')` returns on the main thread, and compare how the result would differ if the worker had been a child process.

defense.title: Choosing threads, processes, or a separate service for CPU-heavy work
defense.focus: The learner decides where CPU-heavy work should run. They justify it against the alternatives on crash isolation, memory use, latency for the user and operational complexity.
defense.check: Your API generates PDF invoices that take 1 to 3 seconds of CPU each, peaking at 50 per minute. Choose between a worker-thread pool, a pool of child processes, and a separate background job service. Justify the choice and name one failure mode each alternative introduces.

concepts.title: Bounded concurrency
concepts.summary: Limiting how much work runs at once so a burst of tasks cannot overwhelm memory, connections, or downstream services.
objectives: Explain under what workload unbounded Promise.all becomes dangerous
Implement or evaluate a concurrency limit using a pool or semaphore
Choose a limit based on downstream capacity and rate limits
misconceptions: Believing more concurrency always means more throughput
Ignoring downstream rate limits and pool sizes
Assuming arrays passed to Promise.all stay small

intro.title: Why Promise.all over a production-sized list can flood a service
intro.focus: Builds the model that Promise.all over `array.map(asyncFn)` starts every call at once, so in-flight work grows with the input. An array that is small in tests can be huge in production.
intro.check: `await Promise.all(customerIds.map(id => fetchInvoice(id)))`. In tests customerIds has 5 entries; in an admin export it has 40,000. Predict how many fetchInvoice calls are started before the first one completes in each case, and name something that could fail first in production.

applied.title: Reading a p-limit wrapper: what actually caps in-flight work
applied.focus: Applies a limiter to realistic fan-out code: how a pool or semaphore lets N tasks run at a time and how that changes total runtime. Also covers the common bug of calling the async function before handing it to the limiter.
applied.check: `const limit = pLimit(10); await Promise.all(ids.map(id => limit(() => fetchInvoice(id))))` runs with 1,000 ids that each take 200ms. Predict the maximum number of in-flight fetches and the approximate total time. Then explain what changes if the code calls `fetchInvoice(id)` first and passes its result to limit.

advanced.title: Picking a limit from a rate-limited API and a shared connection pool
advanced.focus: Derives a limit from what the downstream systems can handle, and shows what fails when a cap ignores them. Other traffic can be starved of pool connections and the API can return 429s. A concurrency cap also does not enforce a per-minute rate.
advanced.check: A sync job calls a partner API limited to 100 requests/minute (about 300ms per call) and writes each result through a 10-connection database pool shared with web traffic. Compare concurrency limits of 5, 20, and 200: which starves the pool, which triggers 429s, and why even a limit of 5 can exceed the per-minute rate.

defense.title: Defending the concurrency limit you chose for this fan-out
defense.focus: The learner justifies a specific limit from what the downstream systems can handle and explains why raising it may not raise throughput. They also weigh alternatives such as fixed-size chunks or queue workers.
defense.check: Defend the concurrency limit in this batch import: what downstream capacity it is derived from, why doubling it might not increase throughput, how runtime and downstream load change if the input grows 100x, and one alternative (fixed-size chunks or queue workers with a concurrency setting) with its tradeoff.

concepts.title: Backpressure
concepts.summary: Signaling producers to slow down when consumers cannot keep up, instead of buffering until something falls over.
objectives: Identify where unbounded buffering occurs between a producer and consumer
Compare dropping, blocking, and rejecting as responses to overload
Design backpressure for a streaming or queue-based pipeline
misconceptions: Believing a bigger buffer or queue fixes sustained overload rather than delaying the failure
Believing a concurrency limiter bounds memory, when tasks waiting for a slot accumulate in an unbounded pending queue
Assuming a stream write is flushed immediately, so its return value can be ignored

intro.title: Where work piles up when producers outrun consumers
intro.focus: Builds the model that when work arrives faster than it is processed, the difference builds up in some buffer. Under sustained overload a bigger buffer only delays the failure.
intro.check: A webhook handler pushes each event onto an in-memory array, and a worker drains it at 50 events/second. Events arrive at 80/second for an hour. Explain where the extra events go, roughly how many accumulate, and why raising the buffer's size limit doesn't fix it.

applied.title: Why ignoring stream write()'s return value can balloon memory
applied.focus: Applies the idea to streams. When `write()` returns false, the internal buffer is past its highWaterMark. If the producer doesn't wait for 'drain' or use pipeline(), data keeps piling up in memory.
applied.check: `for (const row of rows) res.write(JSON.stringify(row))` sends a large export to a slow client, ignoring the return value. Explain what a false return means and where unsent data accumulates, then compare with awaiting the 'drain' event or streaming through pipeline().

advanced.title: Why a concurrency limiter can still run your process out of memory
advanced.focus: Examines the hidden unbounded queue behind a limiter, where waiting tasks pile up. Compares the three responses to overload (drop, block, reject) and what each costs callers.
advanced.check: An endpoint wraps each incoming job in `limit(() => process(job))` with a limit of 10, and jobs arrive faster than they complete. Explain what grows without bound, then compare rejecting with 429 once pending work exceeds N, dropping the oldest pending jobs, and making the producer wait.

defense.title: Defending an overload policy for each hop of a queue pipeline
defense.focus: The learner designs backpressure across the whole pipeline: where buffers are bounded and how each hop signals overload. They defend drop, block or reject at each hop based on whether callers can retry and whether losing data is acceptable.
defense.check: An ingestion API feeds a queue consumed by workers that call a slow enrichment service. Specify where buffers are bounded, what signal slows or rejects producers at each hop, and whether each hop drops, blocks, or rejects. Defend each choice, and explain why simply enlarging the queue is not your answer.

concepts.title: Caching
concepts.summary: Keeping computed or fetched results closer to where they are needed, and deciding when they stop being true.
objectives: Explain cache hit, miss, TTL, and invalidation for a specific cache
Identify data that must never be cached across users
Compare caching layers such as HTTP, CDN, framework, and application memory
misconceptions: Caching personalized responses under a shared key
Believing in-process caches are shared across instances
Adding a cache without an invalidation strategy

intro.title: What a cache returns on a hit, a miss, and after its TTL expires
intro.focus: Builds the model of a cache as a keyed copy of data that can go stale. Covers hits, misses and TTL expiry, and why stale reads continue until the entry expires or is invalidated.
intro.check: `getPrice(id)` checks a Map; on a miss it reads the database and stores the value with a 60-second TTL. The entry is cached at t=0 and the price changes in the database at t=10s. Predict what callers see at t=30s and t=70s, and explain what would have to happen for them to see the new price at t=30s.

applied.title: How a shared cache key can show one user another user's account
applied.focus: Applies cache keys and HTTP caching headers to personalized responses. Covers what must go in the key, when `Cache-Control: private` or no caching is required, and which data must never be cached across users.
applied.check: `GET /api/me` is cached under the key 'me' for 5 minutes (or served with `Cache-Control: public, max-age=300` behind a CDN). Alice requests it, then Bob. Predict what Bob receives and explain what must change in the key or headers.

advanced.title: Why each instance's in-memory cache tells a different story
advanced.focus: Compares caching layers (application memory, a shared store such as Redis, a framework data cache, CDN/HTTP) by who shares the entries and how invalidation reaches them. Includes the edge case of deleting a key on only one instance.
advanced.check: Four instances each keep a module-level LRU of product data with a 10-minute TTL. An admin update calls `cache.delete(productId)` on the one instance that handled it. Describe what users see over the next 10 minutes, then compare with a shared Redis cache with explicit invalidation and with a CDN caching the HTTP response.

defense.title: Defending which layer caches this page and how it gets invalidated
defense.focus: The learner designs a caching plan for a mix of public and personalized data. For each piece they defend the layer, the key, and the TTL or invalidation trigger, and predict what a missed invalidation would do.
defense.check: A product page shows public catalog data and a per-user cart count. Defend where each piece is cached (CDN/HTTP, framework data cache, Redis, or not at all), its cache key and TTL or invalidation trigger, and what users would see if an invalidation event were missed.

concepts.title: Containers
concepts.summary: Packaging an application with its runtime dependencies into an image that runs the same way across environments.
objectives: Explain the difference between an image and a running container
Evaluate a Dockerfile for layer caching, image size, and secret exposure
Identify why a container behaves differently from the developer's machine
misconceptions: Believing containers provide strong security isolation by default, when they share the host kernel
Believing a secret passed via ARG/ENV or deleted in a later RUN step is gone from the final image
Assuming running as root inside a container is harmless because the container is isolated
Assuming the app will stop cleanly on SIGTERM when it runs as PID 1 behind a shell-form CMD or without its own signal handler

intro.title: Image vs container: what's baked in at build and what's lost on removal
intro.focus: Builds the model of an image as a read-only, layered template and a container as a running instance with its own writable layer. A container is an isolated process on the host's kernel, not a separate machine.
intro.check: An app writes uploads to /app/uploads inside its container. The container is removed and a new one is started from the same image. Which uploaded files exist in the new container? Explain using the difference between an image and a container.

applied.title: Why docker stop hangs 10 seconds and cuts off in-flight requests
applied.focus: Applies the model to gaps between a laptop and a container. Covers PID 1 signal handling behind a shell-form CMD, listening on 127.0.0.1 inside the container, and base-image or CPU-architecture differences that affect native dependencies.
applied.check: Locally Ctrl+C stops the server cleanly. In the container, `docker stop` waits about 10 seconds and in-flight requests are cut off. The Dockerfile ends with `CMD npm run start` (shell form) and the app has no SIGTERM handler. Explain which process is PID 1, why the app may never act on SIGTERM, and what happens when the grace period ends.

advanced.title: How a deleted build secret still ships inside your image layers
advanced.focus: Reviews Dockerfiles for secret exposure, layer-cache ordering and image size. Earlier layers and build-arg history stay in the image, so the lesson compares risky patterns with BuildKit secret mounts and multi-stage builds.
advanced.check: Compare (a) `ARG NPM_TOKEN`, `RUN echo "//registry.npmjs.org/:_authToken=$NPM_TOKEN" > .npmrc`, `RUN npm ci`, `RUN rm .npmrc` with (b) `RUN --mount=type=secret,id=npmrc,target=/root/.npmrc npm ci` in a build stage copied into a slim final stage. Explain where the token can still be recovered in (a), and which placement of `COPY . .` keeps the npm ci layer cached.

defense.title: Designing a production Dockerfile you can justify line by line
defense.focus: The learner designs a hardened image and defends choices such as a non-root USER, an exec-form entrypoint with signal handling, and a multi-stage build. They also explain why container isolation alone doesn't make running as root safe.
defense.check: Design a Dockerfile for a Node API covering base image, multi-stage build, dependency layer ordering, a non-root USER, an exec-form entrypoint that handles SIGTERM, and a HEALTHCHECK. Justify running as non-root even though 'the container is isolated', and compare it with running as root but dropping Linux capabilities.

concepts.title: CI/CD pipelines
concepts.summary: Automating build, test, and deploy steps so every change reaches production through the same verified path.
objectives: Trace what a pipeline runs for a pull request versus a merge to main
Identify pipeline steps that expose secrets to untrusted code
Design a deploy sequence that supports rollback
misconceptions: Believing fork pull requests can never reach repository secrets, when pull_request_target and workflow_run run in the base repository's context with secrets and its GITHUB_TOKEN
Believing a green pipeline means the deploy is safe
Believing a version tag such as @v4 on a third-party action is immutable, so pinning to a full commit SHA is unnecessary

intro.title: What your pipeline runs on a pull request versus a merge to main
intro.focus: Builds the model of triggers and jobs: which workflow runs for PR events and which runs for pushes to main. A green check means the configured steps passed, not that the change is safe to deploy.
intro.check: One workflow runs lint and tests `on: pull_request`; another runs tests then a deploy job `on: push` to main. Trace which jobs run when you open a PR, when you push a fix to that PR, and when it is merged.

applied.title: Why a third-party action pinned to @v4 can change without you noticing
applied.focus: Applies supply-chain thinking to workflow steps. Version tags can be moved, so a compromised or repointed action runs with whatever secrets its job exposes. Pinning a full commit SHA fixes which code runs, but doesn't check that the code is safe.
applied.check: A job with `DEPLOY_TOKEN` in its environment uses `some-org/setup-tool@v4`. Explain what happens on your next run if the maintainer's account is compromised and the v4 tag is moved to a malicious commit, and what pinning to a full commit SHA does and does not protect against.

advanced.title: How pull_request_target can hand repository secrets to a fork's code
advanced.focus: Traces the context each trigger runs in. pull_request_target and workflow_run run in the base repository with its secrets and GITHUB_TOKEN, so checking out and running the PR's code exposes them to untrusted contributors.
advanced.check: A workflow on `pull_request_target` checks out `github.event.pull_request.head.sha` and runs `npm install && npm test` with `NPM_TOKEN` available. For a PR from a fork, trace whose code runs, in which repository's context, and what that code can read or do.

defense.title: Designing a deploy where a green build is not the last safeguard
defense.focus: The learner designs a path from merge to production that supports rollback: build once and promote the same artifact, roll out in stages or via canary, and gate on health checks. They explain why passing CI doesn't remove the need for these steps.
defense.check: Design the path from merge to production for a web service: what is built and promoted, how rollout is staged, which health signals gate full rollout, and how you roll back. Explain why a passing test suite doesn't justify skipping these steps, and name one kind of change that makes rollback harder than redeploying the previous artifact.

concepts.title: Distributed failure
concepts.summary: In systems spanning multiple processes and machines, partial failure, duplication, and ambiguous outcomes are normal, not exceptional.
objectives: Explain why a remote call can have three outcomes: success, failure, or unknown
Analyze a workflow spanning a database and an external service for inconsistency windows
Defend a design such as an outbox, saga, or reconciliation job for a specific failure mode
misconceptions: Believing a database transaction also makes an API call or message publish made inside it atomic with the write
Assuming events and webhooks arrive in the order they were produced
Believing a committed local write will reach downstream services without a durable handoff such as an outbox or reconciliation

intro.title: Why a timeout doesn't tell you whether the charge went through
intro.focus: Builds the model that a remote call can succeed, fail, or end with an unknown outcome. Wrapping it in a database transaction does not undo the external side effect when the write rolls back.
intro.check: `await db.transaction(async tx => { await tx.insert(order); await payments.charge(card, amount); })`. The charge call times out after 5 seconds and the transaction rolls back. Explain the possible states of the customer's card and of your orders table.

applied.title: Where the gap opens between your database commit and a downstream call
applied.focus: Applies the model to a realistic write-then-notify path. It locates the window where a crash or failure leaves systems out of sync, which depends on whether the external call happens before or after the commit.
applied.check: A handler commits `status = 'paid'`, then calls `emailService.sendReceipt()` and publishes `order.paid`. Explain what each downstream system knows if the process crashes right after the commit, then compare the inconsistency you get by making the calls before the commit instead.

advanced.title: Why a refund event can be overwritten by the payment it reverses
advanced.focus: Examines events and webhooks that arrive out of order or more than once. Compares ways to keep state correct: per-entity versions or sequence numbers, re-reading the source of truth, or rejecting invalid state transitions.
advanced.check: A consumer handles `order.paid` and `order.refunded` webhooks by setting status to the type of the event it received last. Deliveries are retried and can arrive out of order. Explain how an order ends up 'paid' after being refunded, and compare version checks, fetching current state from the provider, and a transition-validating state machine.

defense.title: Defending an outbox, saga, or reconciliation job for this workflow
defense.focus: The learner picks a durable-handoff or recovery pattern for a named failure. They defend it against the alternatives and state the window of inconsistency that still remains.
defense.check: An order flow writes to your database, charges a card through a payment provider, and notifies a warehouse API. For the failure 'the local write committed but the warehouse was never notified', choose an outbox, a saga with compensating actions, or a reconciliation job (or a combination), defend it against the other two, and state what inconsistency window remains.

concepts.title: Instances and runtime lifecycle
concepts.summary: Production code runs in many replaceable instances — long-running servers, serverless functions, or containers — that start cold, get frozen or terminated, and share nothing in memory.
objectives: Predict whether work started after a response is returned will complete on a serverless versus a long-running runtime
Identify module-level or in-memory state that breaks when requests are served by different instances
Design graceful shutdown that stops accepting work and drains in-flight requests on a termination signal
misconceptions: Believing a serverless function keeps running un-awaited work after the response has been returned
Assuming module-level state persists and is shared across all requests in production
Assuming a process gets unlimited time to finish work after receiving SIGTERM

intro.title: Why your in-memory counter resets and disagrees across instances
intro.focus: Builds the model that production runs several replaceable instances. Each has its own module-level memory that is lost on restart or deploy, so in-memory state is neither shared nor durable.
intro.check: A module-level `let requestCount = 0` is incremented on each request and returned by `/stats`. Production runs 3 instances behind a load balancer and deploys daily. Predict what two consecutive /stats calls might return, and what happens to the count after a deploy.

applied.title: Why the analytics call after returning a response sometimes never runs
applied.focus: Applies runtime lifecycle to work done after the response. A serverless instance may be frozen or shut down once the response is sent, while a long-running server usually keeps going. APIs like waitUntil/after() keep it alive longer, but only within platform limits.
applied.check: A handler calls `trackEvent(user)` without awaiting it and immediately returns a response. Predict whether the tracking request completes on a serverless platform versus a long-running Node server, and explain what wrapping it in `waitUntil` or `after()` changes and what limit still applies.

advanced.title: What happens to in-flight requests when the platform sends SIGTERM
advanced.focus: Examines how shutdown goes wrong: exiting immediately, hanging on idle keep-alive connections, traffic still arriving briefly after the signal, and a hard kill when the grace period ends.
advanced.check: A pod gets SIGTERM with a 30-second grace period. Handler A calls `server.close()` then `process.exit(0)` right away. Handler B stops accepting new connections, waits for in-flight requests, and exits before the deadline. Predict what happens to a 5-second request in flight under each, and what happens to B if a request takes 45 seconds.

defense.title: Designing a service that behaves when instances vanish mid-request
defense.focus: The learner designs the shutdown order and decides where state lives during a rolling deploy. They justify choices such as waitUntil versus a durable job queue for work done after the response.
defense.check: Design how this service handles a rolling deploy: the SIGTERM handler's steps and their order, the drain timeout relative to the platform's grace period, where per-user rate-limit counters currently in a module-level Map should live instead, and whether post-response emails use waitUntil or a durable job queue, with the tradeoff of each.
